```text
source:
  component: default-scheduler
type: Warning
```

Flag `--field-selector` can be used to filter out the output as well. For example, the following command provides events of Pod only:

```bash
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.kind=Pod
```

See the full list of supported `involvedObject` fields [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/common-definitions/object-reference/#ObjectReference).

More fields can be added to the field-selector flag for filtering events further. For example, the following command provides events of the `ps-cluster1-mysql-0` Pod:

```bash
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.kind=Pod,involvedObject.name=ps-cluster1-mysql-0
```

Expected output

```text
LAST SEEN   TYPE      REASON            OBJECT                 MESSAGE
53m         Normal    Created           pod/ps-cluster1-mysql-0   Created container mysql
53m         Normal    Started           pod/ps-cluster1-mysql-0   Started container mysql
53m         Normal    Pulling           pod/ps-cluster1-mysql-0   Pulling image "percona/percona-server-mysql-operator:0.8.0-backup"
...
```

Same way you can query events for other Kubernetes object (StatefulSet, Custom Resource, etc.) to investigate any problems to them:

```bash
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.kind=PerconaServerMySQL,involvedObject.name=ps-cluster1
```

Expected output

```text
LAST SEEN   TYPE      REASON                     OBJECT                        MESSAGE
10m         Warning   AsyncReplicationNotReady   perconaservermysql/ps-cluster1   ps-cluster1-mysql-1: [not_replicating]
...
```

Alternatively, you can see events for a specific object in the output of `kubectl describe` command:

```bash
kubectl describe ps ps-cluster1
```

Expected output

```text
Name:         ps-cluster1
...
Events:
  Type     Reason                    Age                From           Message
  ----     ------                    ----               ----           -------
  Warning  AsyncReplicationNotReady  10m (x23 over 13m)    ps-controller  ps-cluster1-mysql-1: [not_replicating]
...
```

Check `kubectl get events --help` to know about more options.

Note

It is important to note that events are stored in the [etcd](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/#etcd) for only 60 minutes. Ensure that events are checked within 60 minutes of the issue. Kubernetes cluster administrators might also use event exporters for storing the events.

# Check the Logs

Logs provide valuable information. It makes sense to check the logs of the database Pods and the Operator Pod. Following flags are helpful for checking the logs with the `kubectl logs` command:

| Flag                           | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--container=<container-name>` | Print log of a specific container in case of multiple containers in a Pod                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `--follow`                     | Follows the logs for a live output                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `--since=<time>`               | Print logs newer than the specified time, for example: `--since="10s"`                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `--timestamps`                 | Print timestamp in the logs (timezone is taken from the container)                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `--previous`                   | Print previous instantiation of a container. This is extremely useful in case of container restart, where there is a need to check the logs on why the container restarted. Logs of previous instantiation might not be available in all the cases. |

When [persistent logging](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/persistent-logging.md) is enabled, the MySQL error log is written to a file on the data volume and streamed to the `logs` container. It does not appear in the `mysql` container output. Read it with:

```bash
kubectl logs ps-cluster1-mysql-0 -c logs
```

In the following examples we will access containers of the `ps-cluster1-mysql-0` Pod.

- Check logs of the `mysql` container:

  ```bash
  kubectl logs ps-cluster1-mysql-0 -c mysql
  ```

- Check logs of the `xtrabackup` container:

  ```bash
  kubectl logs ps-cluster1-mysql-0 -c xtrabackup
  ```

  See more about troubleshooting backups in the [Troubleshoot backups and restores](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/debug-backup-restore.md) chapter.

- Filter logs of the `mysql` container which are not older than 600 seconds:

  ```bash
  kubectl logs ps-cluster1-mysql-0 -c mysql --since=600s
  ```

- Check logs of a previous instantiation of the `mysql` container, if any:

  ```bash
  kubectl logs ps-cluster1-mysql-0 -c mysql --previous
  ```

- Check logs of the `mysql` container for `ERROR` messages:

  ```bash
  kubectl logs ps-cluster1-mysql-0 -c mysql | grep 'ERROR'
  ```

- Check logs of the Operator:

  ```bash
  kubectl logs -l "app.kubernetes.io/name=percona-server-mysql-operator" --tail=-1
  ```

- Check logs of the operator, parsing the output with [jq JSON processor](https://stedolan.github.io/jq/) (requires `LOG_STRUCTURED` to be `true`):

  ```bash
  kubectl logs -l "app.kubernetes.io/name=percona-server-mysql-operator" --tail=-1 -f | jq -R 'fromjson?'
  ```

- Check logs of the HAProxy pod for configuration issues:

  ```bash
  kubectl logs ps-cluster1-haproxy-0 | grep 'The custom config /etc/haproxy-custom/haproxy.cfg is not valid and will be ignored.'
  ```

# Troubleshoot backups and restores

You can troubleshoot failed backups or restores by checking the status of backup and restore objects, examining the jobs that executed them, and reviewing logs from the jobs and /or the pods created by the Jobs.

The overall troubleshooting workflow looks like this:

1. Check the object status. Use `kubectl get ps-backup` or `kubectl get ps-restore` to see the current state.
1. Review error details. Use `kubectl describe` to get the error message from the `State Description` field.
1. Examine job logs. Check the logs from the backup or restore job for detailed execution information.
1. Check source pod logs. For backups, review logs from the `xtrabackup` container in the source pod. For restores, view logs of the Pod created by the restore Job.
1. Verify configuration. Ensure storage configurations, credentials, and cluster settings are correct.

Refer to the following sections for details. For status field reference, see [Custom resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/cr-statuses.md).

## Backups

### Check backup status

Start by checking the status of your backup objects:

```bash
kubectl get ps-backup -n <namespace>
```

This shows you all backup objects with their current state. The `STATE` column indicates whether a backup succeeded, failed, or is in progress.

Example output

```text
NAME                                           STORAGE      DESTINATION                                                  STATE       COMPLETED   AGE
backup1                                        aws-s3       s3://operator-testing/ps-cluster1-2025-11-07-20:59:28-full   Succeeded   11m         11m
backup2                                        azure                                                                     Error                   10m
backup3                                        azure-blob   operator-testing/ps-cluster1-2025-11-07-21:00:14-full        Succeeded   10m         10m
backup4                                        gcp-cs       s3://operator-testing/ps-cluster1-2025-11-07-21:01:19-full   Succeeded   3m37s       9m29s
backup5                                        gcp-cs       s3://operator-testing/ps-cluster1-2025-11-07-21:07:20-full   Succeeded   3m17s       3m28s
cron-ps-cluster1-aws-s3-20251107211029-45srk   aws-s3       s3://operator-testing/ps-cluster1-2025-11-07-21:10:29-full   Succeeded
```

### Check backup error details

When a backup fails, use `kubectl describe` to get detailed error information:

```bash
kubectl describe ps-backup <backup-name> -n <namespace>
```

The `Status` section contains the `State` and `State Description` fields that explain why the backup failed.

Example error output

```text
Name:         backup2
Namespace:    default
...
Status:
  State:              Error
  State Description:  azure not found in spec.backup.storages in PerconaServerMySQL CustomResource
Events:               <none>
```

Common error scenarios include:

- **Storage not found**: The storage name specified in the backup doesn’t exist in the cluster configuration
- **Authentication failures**: Invalid credentials for accessing cloud storage
- **Network issues**: Problems connecting to the storage service
- **Insufficient permissions**: The backup job doesn’t have permission to write to the storage location
- **TLS certificate errors**: The storage endpoint uses a private CA and the Operator cannot verify it. Typical Job or sidecar log messages include `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` or `certificate verify failed`. Keep `verifyTLS` enabled, confirm `crVersion` is `1.3.0` or later, and supply the CA with [`s3.caBundle`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-storage.md#configure-tls-verification-with-custom-certificates-for-s3-storage).

### Check backup Jobs

When a backup runs, the Operator creates a Kubernetes Job to execute it. You can view these Jobs to see which backups are running or have completed:

```bash
kubectl get jobs -n <namespace>
```

Backup jobs follow this naming pattern:

- `xb-<backup-name>-<storage-name>` for on-demand backups
- `xb-cron-<cluster-name>-<storage-name>-<timestamp>-<hash>-<storage-name>` for scheduled backups

Example output

```text
NAME                                                     STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
xb-backup1-aws-s3                                        Complete   1/1           14s        11m
xb-backup3-azure-blob                                    Complete   1/1           12s        10m
xb-backup4-gcp-cs                                        Complete   1/1           5m52s      9m45s
xb-backup5-gcp-cs                                        Complete   1/1           10s        3m43s
xb-cron-ps-cluster1-aws-s3-20251107211029-45srk-aws-s3   Complete   1/1           12s        35s
```

### View backup job logs

To see detailed logs from a backup job, use the job name:

```bash
kubectl logs job/<job-name> -n <namespace>
```

Find the name using the steps from the [Check backup Jobs](#check-backup-jobs) section

For example, to view logs from the `xb-backup1-aws-s3` job:

```bash
kubectl logs job/xb-backup1-aws-s3 -n <namespace>
```

These logs show the backup process execution, including Percona XtraBackup operations and any errors that occurred.

Example output


You can also view logs from the Pod created by the Job:

```bash
kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace>
```

To find the Pod name, list pods and look for pods with names matching your backup job:

```bash
kubectl get pods -n <namespace> | grep xb-
```

### Find the backup source Pod

Each backup object contains information about which MySQL Pod was used as the backup source. You can retrieve this information using:

```bash
kubectl get ps-backup <backup-name> -o jsonpath='{.status.backupSource}' -n <namespace>
```

For example:

```bash
kubectl get ps-backup backup1 -o jsonpath='{.status.backupSource}'
```

This returns the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of the source pod, such as `ps-cluster1-mysql-1.ps-cluster1-mysql.default`.

### View backup logs from the source pod

The `xtrabackup` container in the source pod also contains backup logs. To view them, run:

```bash
kubectl logs <source-pod-name> -c xtrabackup -n <namespace>
```

For example, if the backup source is `ps-cluster1-mysql-1`:

```bash
kubectl logs ps-cluster1-mysql-1 -c xtrabackup -n <namespace>
```

These logs show the backup request received by the sidecar container, including the backup destination, storage type, and Percona XtraBackup commands executed.

## Restores

### Check restore status

To check the status of restore operations, run:

```bash
kubectl get ps-restore -n <namespace>
```

This shows all restore objects with their current state.

Example output

```text
NAME       STATE       AGE
restore1   Error       5m56s
restore2   Succeeded   5m37s
```

### Check restore error details

When a restore fails, use the `kubectl describe` command to get detailed error information:

```bash
kubectl describe ps-restore <restore-name> -n <namespace>
```

The `Status` section contains the `State` and `State Description` fields that explain why the restore failed.

Example error output

```text
Name:         restore1
Namespace:    default
...
Status:
  State:              Error
  State Description:  PerconaServerMySQLBackup backup11 in namespace default is not found
Events:               <none>
```

Example success output

```text
Name:         restore2
Namespace:    default
...
Status:
  State:  Succeeded
Events:   <none>
```

Common restore error scenarios include:

- **Backup not found**: The backup specified in the restore doesn’t exist
- **Storage access issues**: Problems reading from the backup storage location
- **Cluster state conflicts**: The cluster is not in a state that allows restore
- **Insufficient resources**: Not enough disk space or memory to complete the restore
- **TLS certificate errors**: The restore Job cannot verify the S3 endpoint certificate. See [Restore from S3 storage that uses a custom CA](#restore-from-s3-storage-that-uses-a-custom-ca).

### Check restore jobs

When a restore runs, the Operator creates a Kubernetes Job to execute it. View these Jobs:

```bash
kubectl get jobs -n <namespace>
```

Restore jobs follow the naming pattern `xb-restore-<restore-name>`.

Example output

```text
NAME                                                     STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE

```

### View restore job logs

To see detailed logs from a restore Job, run:

```bash

```

For example:

```bash

```

Sample output

## Point-in-time recovery

Point-in-time recovery adds a Binlog Server Pod and a PITR Job (`pitr-restore-<restore-name>`) on top of the base restore Job (`xb-restore-<restore-name>`). Check both Jobs and the Binlog Server Pod, not only `xb-restore-*`.

To inspect the restored base backup before the binary logs are applied, see [Pause a point-in-time recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/pause-pitr.md).

### Binlog Server is in CrashLoopBackOff

If the binlog bucket contains too many objects, Binlog Server can get stuck listing them and enter the CrashLoopBackOff state. Point-in-time recovery cannot proceed until the Pod is healthy.

Delete old binlog objects from the bucket so the object count drops. If you miss the binlog expiration window, restore becomes much harder. Monitor object count in the point-in-time recovery bucket and clean up regularly.

### Restore fails after the base backup is already restored

Point-in-time recovery retries are not idempotent. If the PITR Job fails after the base backup is on disk, a retry does not restore that backup again to reset the state.

Set `spec.backup.backoffLimit=0` in the cluster Custom Resource so the Job does not retry automatically. Fix the cause, then start a new restore from a known-good base backup.

### Replication errors during binlog replay

Updates made by `mysql-shell` can produce errors such as `Error_code: 1032` / `HA_ERR_KEY_NOT_FOUND` on `mysql_innodb_cluster_metadata.instances`.

If you choose to ignore SQL errors, add `force: true` under `spec.pitr` in the restore object. This passes `--force` to the MySQL client and silently ignores **all** SQL errors during replay, which can hide data loss. See [Ignore SQL errors during binlog replay](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-restore-pitr.md#ignore-sql-errors-during-binlog-replay).

### Encrypted binlogs fail to decrypt

The PITR Job cannot unwrap a binlog if the mounted keyring does not contain the KEK recorded in that file.

Typical causes:

- Restore to a new cluster without `spec.pitr.keyringSecret`
- Keys rotated into another Secret, but the restore still uses the cluster keyring
- A KEK removed from `keyring.json`

Check the PITR Job logs (`pitr-restore-<restore-name>`) for KEK / keyring errors. To copy the Secret and set `keyringSecret`, see [Restore with encrypted binlogs](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-restore-pitr.md#restore-with-encrypted-binlogs). Lost keys cannot be recovered.

### Operator user password changed after the backup

If the Operator user password in the live cluster differs from the password stored in the base backup, point-in-time recovery fails. Take a new full backup after you change that password, then restore from the new backup.

## Restore from S3 storage that uses a custom CA

If restore Job logs show `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority`, `certificate verify failed`, or a similar TLS error, the S3-compatible endpoint is presenting a certificate your cluster does not trust.

Do not set `verifyTLS: false` or `VERIFY_TLS=false` to work around this. Instead, supply the CA and keep verification enabled.

1. Confirm the Operator version and Custom Resource version are `1.3.0` or later. If you upgraded the Operator but left `spec.crVersion` at `1.2.0`, the Operator ignores `caBundle`.
1. Confirm `caBundle.name` and `caBundle.key` match the Secret that holds the CA.
1. Confirm the CA Secret exists in the namespace where the restore runs. Create it from the CA file if you are restoring on a new cluster.
1. Set `caBundle` on the restore object. For a backup-only restore, set it on `spec.backupSource.storage.s3`. For point-in-time recovery, also set it on `spec.pitr.backupSource.binlogServer.storage.s3`.

On the same cluster with `backupName`, the Operator can use `caBundle` already set on the cluster Custom Resource.

See [Configure TLS verification with custom certificates for S3 storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-storage.md#configure-tls-verification-with-custom-certificates-for-s3-storage), [Restore from S3 storage that uses a custom CA](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-restore-to-new-cluster.md#restore-from-s3-storage-that-uses-a-custom-ca), and [Use a custom CA](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-restore-pitr.md#use-a-custom-ca) for point-in-time recovery.

# Recover from a full cluster crash

A full cluster crash happens when the majority of members in a cluster with [Group Replication](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/architecture.md#group-replication) (GR) are down and the group loses quorum. Even if the primary is among the survivors, the group can’t vote, so after a short timeout, the primary enters the error state too. A power loss in the data center, deletion of MySQL Pods, or an out-of-memory kill can take down enough members to cause this. After the Pods restart, no member can form the group on its own, because none of them knows if it has the most recent data.

The Operator detects this situation and recovers the cluster automatically if the `spec.mysql.autoRecovery` is set to `true`. This page explains how to recognize a full cluster crash, how to track the recovery, what to do when you disable automatic recovery or when it doesn’t succeed, and how the recovery works.

This page applies to clusters with Group Replication, the default replication type. Clusters with [asynchronous replication](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/architecture.md#asynchronous-replication-tech-preview) don’t use this mechanism, and the `mysql.autoRecovery` option has no effect on them. After all MySQL Pods restart, Orchestrator restores the replication topology without manual steps. For details, see [Zero data loss failover in async clusters](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/failover-async.md).

Note

Pausing a cluster with Group Replication and starting it again goes through the same recovery, because all members stop at the same time. See [Pause/resume the cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/pause.md). Keep automatic recovery enabled, or be ready to follow the [manual steps](#recover-the-cluster-manually) after every resume.

## Symptoms

A cluster is in a full cluster crash when you see the following:

- `kubectl get ps <cluster-name> -n <namespace>` shows the `error` state, and the cluster condition has the `FullClusterCrashDetected` reason.
- `kubectl describe ps <cluster-name> -n <namespace>` shows the `FullClusterCrashDetected` warning event (`Full cluster crash detected`).
- The log of the `mysql` container in the MySQL Pods contains a message between two `######FULL_CLUSTER_CRASH:<Pod FQDN>######` lines.
- The MySQL Pods are `Ready`, but your applications can’t write to the database, because the cluster has no primary.

## Choose what to do

Check whether automatic recovery is enabled:

```bash
kubectl get ps <cluster-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.mysql.autoRecovery}'
```

An empty output means that the option isn’t set, and the Operator treats it as `false`.

| Situation                                   | What to do                                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `mysql.autoRecovery` is `true`              | The Operator recovers the cluster. [Track the recovery](#track-the-recovery). |
| `mysql.autoRecovery` is `false` or not set  | [Recover the cluster manually](#recover-the-cluster-manually).                |
| The recovery doesn’t start or keeps failing | [Troubleshoot the recovery](#troubleshoot-the-recovery).                      |

## Recover the cluster automatically

The `mysql.autoRecovery` option in the Custom Resource controls the automatic recovery. The `deploy/cr.yaml` and `deploy/cr-minimal.yaml` files set it to `true`. If you omit the option in your own Custom Resource, the Operator treats it as `false`, so set it explicitly:

```yaml
spec:
  mysql:
    clusterType: group-replication
    autoRecovery: true
```

The Operator starts the recovery only when all MySQL Pods exist and are `Ready`. Make sure that all Pods are scheduled and running. Because the Pods start one after another and each one restarts once before it becomes `Ready`, the recovery takes several minutes even for a small cluster. Recovery time also depends on the cluster size and the amount of data the members must catch up on.

For the steps that the Operator takes, see [What the Operator does during the automatic recovery](#what-the-operator-does-during-the-automatic-recovery).

### Track the recovery

1. Check the cluster state and conditions:

   ```bash
   kubectl get ps <cluster-name> -n <namespace>
   kubectl get ps <cluster-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'
   ```

   The state is `error` with the reason `FullClusterCrashDetected` while the crash is detected. After the reboot, the state changes to `initializing` while the secondary members restart and rejoin, and then to `ready`.

1. List the events of the cluster:

   ```bash
   kubectl describe ps <cluster-name> -n <namespace>
   ```

   Look for the `FullClusterCrashDetected` warning event (`Full cluster crash detected`) and the `FullClusterCrashRecovered` normal event (`Cluster recovered from full cluster crash`). See [Events](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/cr-statuses.md#events) for all events.

1. Check the Operator logs. The following messages show the progress:

   ```bash
   kubectl logs deploy/percona-server-mysql-operator -n <namespace> | grep -i "crash recovery"
   ```

   - `Pod is waiting for recovery` - the Operator found the `full-cluster-crash` file in the Pod. The message includes the Pod name and its `GTID_EXECUTED` value.
   - `Cluster is online, restarting crashed members` - the cluster was already online. The Operator then logs `Deleting pod with stale full cluster crash marker` for each Pod that it restarts.
   - `Attempting to reboot cluster from complete outage` - the Operator runs the reboot command on the Pod.
   - `failed to reboot cluster from complete outage` - the reboot failed on this Pod. The Operator tries the next one.
   - `Cluster was successfully rebooted` - the reboot succeeded.
   - `Primary pod detected` and `Deleting secondary pod` - the Operator restarts the secondary members so that they rejoin the cluster.

## Recover the cluster manually

Recover the cluster manually when `mysql.autoRecovery` is `false`, or when the automatic recovery doesn’t succeed. In the `false` case, the Operator only writes the following error to its log on every reconciliation:

```text
Full cluster crash detected but auto recovery is not enabled.
Enable .spec.mysql.autoRecovery or recover cluster manually
(connect to one of the pods using mysql-shell and run 'dba.rebootClusterFromCompleteOutage() and delete /var/lib/mysql/full-cluster-crash in each pod.').
```

To recover the cluster, do the following:

1. Make sure that all MySQL Pods are running and are `Ready`:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -l app.kubernetes.io/component=database
   ```

1. Optionally, check the `GTID_EXECUTED` value saved in each Pod. The Pod with the most transactions has the most recent data:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-0 -n <namespace> -c mysql -- cat /var/lib/mysql/full-cluster-crash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-1 -n <namespace> -c mysql -- cat /var/lib/mysql/full-cluster-crash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-2 -n <namespace> -c mysql -- cat /var/lib/mysql/full-cluster-crash
   ```

   You can run the reboot on any Pod. MySQL Shell checks all members and starts the group from the one with the most transactions.

1. Get the password of the `root` user from the Secret that you set in the `spec.secretsName` option (`<cluster-name>-secrets` by default):

   ```bash
   kubectl get secret <cluster-name>-secrets -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.data.root}' | base64 --decode
   ```

1. Connect to a MySQL Pod using MySQL Shell in JavaScript mode:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec -it <cluster-name>-mysql-0 -n <namespace> -c mysql -- mysqlsh --js -u root -p
   ```

   Enter the password from the previous step when MySQL Shell asks for it. The `--js` flag is required, because MySQL Shell in the container starts in SQL mode by default. Don’t pass the password in a `root:<password>@localhost` URI: the generated passwords contain special characters that MySQL Shell rejects in a URI.

1. Reboot the cluster:

   ```javascript
   dba.rebootClusterFromCompleteOutage()
   ```

   MySQL Shell prints `The Cluster was successfully rebooted.` when it finishes. If you run the command on a Pod that doesn’t have the most transactions, MySQL Shell reports that it switches over to the instance with the highest GTID set and uses it to start the group. If the command fails with an error, exit and repeat steps 4 and 5 on another Pod.

1. Check that all members are `ONLINE`:

   ```javascript
   dba.getCluster().status()
   ```

   Then exit MySQL Shell with `\quit`.

1. Delete the `full-cluster-crash` file in every Pod. The cluster stays in the `error` state until the file is gone:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-0 -n <namespace> -c mysql -- rm /var/lib/mysql/full-cluster-crash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-1 -n <namespace> -c mysql -- rm /var/lib/mysql/full-cluster-crash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-2 -n <namespace> -c mysql -- rm /var/lib/mysql/full-cluster-crash
   ```

   Delete the file only after the reboot succeeds. If you delete it earlier, the `mysql` containers restart and create the file again.

1. Wait until the cluster reaches the `ready` state:

   ```bash
   kubectl get ps <cluster-name> -n <namespace>
   ```

You don’t need to delete the secondary Pods after a manual recovery. MySQL Shell rejoins them to the cluster during the reboot.

## Troubleshoot the recovery

The recovery doesn’t start:

- Check that all MySQL Pods exist and are `Ready`. The Operator doesn’t act on a partially started cluster and doesn’t log anything about the recovery while a Pod is missing. Because Pods start one at a time, a single Pod that can’t start blocks all Pods after it. If a Pod is missing, check the events of the StatefulSet:

  ```bash
  kubectl describe statefulset <cluster-name>-mysql -n <namespace>
  ```

- Check the Operator logs for the `Full cluster crash detected but auto recovery is not enabled` error. If you see it, either enable `mysql.autoRecovery` or recover the cluster [manually](#recover-the-cluster-manually).

- Check that the Operator Pod is running. While the Operator is down, `kubectl get ps` shows the last state that the Operator reported, which can be `ready`. The recovery starts after the Operator is back.

The recovery keeps failing:

- Look for the `failed to reboot cluster from complete outage` messages in the Operator logs. They contain the error returned by MySQL Shell.
- Check the log of the `mysql` containers for the reason that the member can’t join the group.
- [Recover the cluster manually](#recover-the-cluster-manually) and use the error from MySQL Shell to choose the Pod to run the reboot on.

## How full cluster crash recovery works

### How the Operator detects a full cluster crash

1. MySQL Pods start one at a time: Kubernetes creates the next Pod only after the previous one is `Ready`. Every MySQL Pod tries to find a member of the cluster to join. When it can’t reach any peer, the Pod reads its `GTID_EXECUTED` value (the set of global transaction identifiers it has applied) and saves it to the `/var/lib/mysql/full-cluster-crash` file. Then the `mysql` container restarts.
1. The container sees the file at startup and keeps `mysqld` running in read-only mode. It prints a message between two `######FULL_CLUSTER_CRASH:<Pod FQDN>######` lines to its log, where `<Pod FQDN>` is the fully qualified domain name of the Pod, for example, `ps-cluster1-mysql-0.ps-cluster1-mysql.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. The message contains the last `GTID_EXECUTED` value of that Pod. The Pods report the `Ready` state in this mode, so that you and the Operator can connect to them.
1. As soon as a `Ready` MySQL Pod has the file, the Operator sets the cluster `status.state` to `error`, adds a condition with the `FullClusterCrashDetected` reason, and records the `FullClusterCrashDetected` warning event. The Operator records this event again on every reconciliation until the crash is resolved.

### What the Operator does during the automatic recovery

When automatic recovery is enabled and all MySQL Pods are `Ready`, the Operator does the following:

1. Asks the Pods that don’t have the `full-cluster-crash` file whether the cluster is online. Starting with version 1.3.0, if the cluster is online, the Operator removes the file from the other Pods and restarts these Pods so that they rejoin the cluster. No further steps are needed.
1. If the cluster is not online, picks a Pod with the `full-cluster-crash` file and runs the `dba.rebootClusterFromCompleteOutage()` command from [MySQL Shell](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/mysql-shell/8.4/en/) on it. The Operator doesn’t compare the `GTID_EXECUTED` values to choose the Pod: MySQL Shell finds the member with the most transactions and uses it to start the group. If the command fails on this Pod, the Operator logs the error and tries the next Pod.
1. After the reboot succeeds, records the `FullClusterCrashRecovered` event and removes the `full-cluster-crash` file from every Pod.
1. Waits for the cluster to elect the primary Pod and deletes all other MySQL Pods. Kubernetes recreates them, and they rejoin the cluster as secondary members.

## Related options and events

- [`mysql.autoRecovery`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/operator.md#mysqlautorecovery) - enables or disables the automatic recovery.
- [`FullClusterCrashDetected` condition reason and event](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/cr-statuses.md#conditions)
- [`FullClusterCrashRecovered` event](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/cr-statuses.md#events)
- [The `full-cluster-crash` file](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/datadir-special-files.md#full-cluster-crash) and other special files in the data directory

# Special files in the data directory

The `mysql` container of every MySQL Pod checks for several marker files in its data directory, `/var/lib/mysql`. When one of these files exists, the container, its probes, or the Operator change their behavior. For example, the container may not start `mysqld`, or the Pod may skip joining the cluster.

The data directory is on the Pod’s Persistent Volume. So these files stay in place when the Pod or the container restarts. They are removed only when you or the Operator delete them.

Use another container if `mysql` keeps crashing

The commands on this page use the `mysql` container (`-c mysql`). If this container crashes or restarts in a loop, `kubectl exec` into it can fail. The `xtrabackup` and `logs` containers of the same Pod mount the same data volume at `/var/lib/mysql`, so you can run the commands there instead. The `xtrabackup` container exists when backups are enabled (`backup.enabled`), and the `logs` container exists when [persistent logging](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/persistent-logging.md) is enabled (`logcollector.enabled`). For example:

```bash
kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c xtrabackup -- touch /var/lib/mysql/sleep-forever
```

This page describes:

- [files you can create or remove](#files-you-can-create-or-remove) to debug a Pod: `sleep-forever` and `no-bootstrap`, and the `full-cluster-crash` file that the Operator creates
- the [`percona.com/pitr-sleep-forever` annotation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/pause-pitr.md) to pause a point-in-time recovery
- [files that the Operator manages](#files-managed-by-the-operator), which you must leave alone

## How the files affect the MySQL Pod

Three components of the `mysql` container read the files:

- The entry point script runs when the container starts and then starts `mysqld`.
- The startup probe (`/opt/percona/bootstrap`) configures replication. It clones data from another member if needed and adds the Pod to the cluster.
- The liveness and readiness probes (`/opt/percona/healthcheck`) report the health of `mysqld` to Kubernetes.

The following table shows what each file changes:

| File                 | `mysqld` runs          | Startup probe (clone, join the cluster) | Liveness and readiness probes                                         |
| -------------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sleep-forever`      | No                     | Skipped                                 | Always pass                                                           |
| `no-bootstrap`       | Yes, in read-only mode | Skipped                                 | Always pass                                                           |
| `full-cluster-crash` | Yes, in read-only mode | Skipped                                 | Liveness always passes. Readiness passes as soon as `mysqld` is ready |

## Files you can create or remove

### `sleep-forever`

Use this file to stop a MySQL Pod from starting `mysqld`, while keeping the container running so that you can exec into it. It works for both asynchronous replication and Group Replication.

**What it does**

The entry point script checks for the file when the container starts, before it starts `mysqld`. If the file exists, the script prints the following messages to the container log and doesn’t start `mysqld`:

```text
The /var/lib/mysql/sleep-forever file is detected, node is going to infinity loop
If you want to exit from infinity loop you need to remove /var/lib/mysql/sleep-forever file
```

The script then checks every 3 seconds if the file still exists. When you remove the file, the script exits, and Kubernetes restarts the container. The container then starts as usual.

While the file exists, the startup, liveness, and readiness probes pass right away. The Pod doesn’t clone data, join the cluster, or configure replication.

**Who creates or removes it**

You do. The Operator doesn’t create this file for MySQL Pods, with one exception: a [paused point-in-time recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/pause-pitr.md) creates it on the data volume of the `<cluster-name>-mysql-0` Pod. The [`clusterset-recovery` file](#files-managed-by-the-operator) removes `sleep-forever` from a Pod.

**How to use it**

Creating the file in a running container doesn’t stop `mysqld`. It only turns off the probes and the startup bootstrap for this Pod. The container stops before `mysqld` the next time it starts. See [Pause a Pod for debugging](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/pause-mysql-pod.md#pause-a-pod-for-debugging) for the steps.

Because the readiness probe passes right away, you can also use the file to [unblock a rolling update](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/pause-mysql-pod.md#unblock-a-stuck-rolling-update) that waits for an unready Pod.

Warning

- A Pod with the `sleep-forever` file reports `Ready` even though `mysqld` isn’t running, because the readiness probe always passes. Kubernetes Services that select `Ready` Pods may list this Pod. Clients that connect to it fail.
- A rolling update treats this Pod as updated as soon as it reports `Ready` and continues to the next Pod, even though this Pod doesn’t run `mysqld`. The cluster has one less working member until you remove the file.

### `no-bootstrap`

Use this file when `mysqld` must run, for example to run SQL statements by hand, but the startup probe must not clone data, join the cluster, or configure replication, and the liveness probe must not restart the container if `mysqld` stops responding. The file doesn’t stop the Operator or Orchestrator from managing the cluster. It works for both asynchronous replication and Group Replication.

**What it does**

The entry point script ignores this file, so `mysqld` starts as usual. The probes check the file:

- The startup probe exits right away. The Pod doesn’t clone data, join the cluster or the group, or configure replication.
- The liveness and readiness probes always pass. Kubernetes doesn’t restart the container because of failed probes. If the `mysqld` process exits, the container still restarts.

**Who creates or removes it**

You do. The Operator neither creates nor removes this file for MySQL Pods.

**How to use it**

1. Create the file:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c mysql -- touch /var/lib/mysql/no-bootstrap
   ```

1. Delete the Pod so that it starts again with the file in place:

   ```bash
   kubectl delete pod <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace>
   ```

1. Do your work in the Pod.

1. Remove the file:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c mysql -- rm /var/lib/mysql/no-bootstrap
   ```

1. Delete the Pod again. The startup probe runs only when the container starts, so the Pod rejoins the cluster only after a restart:

   ```bash
   kubectl delete pod <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace>
   ```

Warning

A Pod with the `no-bootstrap` file reports `Ready` even if `mysqld` doesn’t work.

### `full-cluster-crash`

This file is used only in clusters with Group Replication. It marks a Pod that waits for recovery after a [full cluster crash](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/crash-recovery.md).

**Who creates or removes it**

The startup probe creates the file when it decides that the group must be rebooted with the `dba.rebootClusterFromCompleteOutage()` command. For example, it does so when the Pod can’t reach any other member of the cluster, or when the cluster has no `ONLINE` primary. The file contains the `GTID_EXECUTED` value of the Pod. After that, the container restarts.

The Operator removes the file from every Pod when it recovers the cluster automatically. If [automatic recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/crash-recovery.md#recover-the-cluster-automatically) is turned off, you remove the file yourself as part of the [manual recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/crash-recovery.md#recover-the-cluster-manually).

**What it does**

While the file exists:

- The entry point script starts `mysqld` in read-only mode. It prints the `GTID_EXECUTED` value of the Pod and the recovery instructions between the `######FULL_CLUSTER_CRASH:<Pod name>######` lines in the container log.
- The startup probe exits right away.
- The liveness probe always passes. The readiness probe passes as soon as `mysqld` is ready, without checking the Group Replication membership. This lets all Pods become `Ready`, so that the Operator can start the recovery.
- The Operator sets the cluster `status.state` to `error` with the `FullClusterCrashDetected` condition reason and records the `FullClusterCrashDetected` event.

See [Recover from a full cluster crash](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/crash-recovery.md) for how to recover the cluster.

Warning

Remove the file from **every** Pod after the cluster is recovered. If you leave it on a Pod, that Pod starts `mysqld` in read-only mode and skips joining the cluster every time it restarts.

## Files managed by the Operator

You may see the following files in `/var/lib/mysql`. The Operator and its tools create and use them. Don’t create, edit, or delete them. The Version column shows the Operator version that added the file. “All” means the file is used in all versions covered by this documentation.

| File                         | Version | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `server-id`                  | 1.3.0   | Stores the `server_id` of this data directory. **Don’t delete it.** Without it, `mysqld` gets a different `server_id` that is based on the Pod number. This can make replication skip transactions without any error.                                                                                                                                              |
| `clusterset-recovery`        | 1.2.0   | The Operator creates it when it removes a Group Replication cluster from a ClusterSet. While it exists, the Operator doesn’t start the full cluster crash recovery. The next time the startup probe runs, it removes this file and also the `sleep-forever`, `no-bootstrap`, and `full-cluster-crash` files. **Don’t create it by hand**, or you lose these files. |
| `bootstrap.lock`             | All     | Exists while the entry point script initializes the data directory. Starting with version 1.3.0, it also exists while the script updates the system users. The startup probe waits until it is removed.                                                                                                                                                            |
| `clone.lock`                 | All     | Created by the startup probe in clusters with asynchronous replication after the Pod clones data from another member, before the container restarts. The startup probe removes it on the next start.                                                                                                                                                               |
| `cr-version`                 | 1.3.0   | Stores the version of the Custom Resource. When it changes, the entry point script updates the system users and their grants.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `failover.lock`              | 1.3.0   | Used during a failover in clusters with asynchronous replication, so that only one failover runs at a time. Don’t open or lock it with other tools. This makes the failover fail.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `mysql.state`, `notify.sock` | All     | Report the state of `mysqld` to the probes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `source-logs/`               | 1.3.0   | Binary logs fetched from the failed primary during a failover in clusters with asynchronous replication.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

### Log files

The following files contain logs that help you troubleshoot a Pod. You can read them safely:

- `bootstrap.log` - the log of the startup probe
- `mysql-state-monitor.log` - the log of the tool that tracks the `mysqld` state
- `pre-stop.log` - the log of the pre-stop hook
- `failover.log` - the log of failover workers in clusters with asynchronous replication, starting with version 1.3.0
- `log/` - the directory for [persistent logs](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/persistent-logging.md), starting with version 1.3.0

For example:

```bash
kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c mysql -- cat /var/lib/mysql/bootstrap.log
```

# Pause a MySQL Pod

Use the `sleep-forever` file in `/var/lib/mysql` when you need the MySQL container to stay up without `mysqld`, or when an unready Pod must report `Ready` so a rolling update can continue. See [`sleep-forever`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/datadir-special-files.md#sleep-forever) for what the file changes.

Use another container if `mysql` keeps crashing

The commands on this page use the `mysql` container (`-c mysql`). If this container crashes or restarts in a loop, `kubectl exec` into it can fail. The `xtrabackup` and `logs` containers of the same Pod mount the same data volume at `/var/lib/mysql`, so you can run the commands there instead. The `xtrabackup` container exists when backups are enabled (`backup.enabled`), and the `logs` container exists when [persistent logging](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/persistent-logging.md) is enabled (`logcollector.enabled`). For example:

```bash
kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c xtrabackup -- touch /var/lib/mysql/sleep-forever
```

## Pause a Pod for debugging

Use the `sleep-forever` file to keep a MySQL Pod running without `mysqld`. This helps when `mysqld` crashes at startup and the container restarts in a loop, or when you need to inspect, repair, or copy files from the data directory while `mysqld` is stopped.

1. Create the file in the `mysql` container of the Pod:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c mysql -- touch /var/lib/mysql/sleep-forever
   ```

   If the `mysql` container restarts too often to run the command, run it in the `xtrabackup` or `logs` container instead. Those containers mount the same data volume. The file is on the Persistent Volume, so it stays in place after the next restart.

1. Delete the Pod. Kubernetes recreates it, and the container stops before starting `mysqld`:

   ```bash
   kubectl delete pod <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace>
   ```

1. Check the container log for the `node is going to infinity loop` message:

   ```bash
   kubectl logs <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c mysql
   ```

1. Open a shell in the container and do your work. The data directory is available in `/var/lib/mysql`:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec -it <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c mysql -- bash
   ```

1. Remove the file to resume the Pod:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c mysql -- rm /var/lib/mysql/sleep-forever
   ```

   In a few seconds, the container exits and Kubernetes restarts it. The container then starts `mysqld`, and the Pod rejoins the cluster.

## Unblock a stuck rolling update

When you change the Custom Resource or upgrade the database, the MySQL Pods restart one by one with the new configuration. Both the `SmartUpdate` and the `RollingUpdate` [update strategies](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/operator.md#updatestrategy) restart the next Pod only when all MySQL Pods are `Ready`. If one Pod is stuck in the unready state, for example because `mysqld` can’t join the cluster, the update stops and waits for this Pod. The update may be the fix for the Pod, but it never reaches the Pod.

The `sleep-forever` file makes the readiness probe pass right away, so the update can continue:

1. Find the Pod that isn’t `Ready`:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -l app.kubernetes.io/component=mysql
   ```

1. Create the file in the `mysql` container of this Pod:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c mysql -- touch /var/lib/mysql/sleep-forever
   ```

   The Pod becomes `Ready` with the next readiness probe, without a restart. The update continues. When it reaches this Pod, the Pod is recreated with the new configuration and doesn’t start `mysqld`.

1. Check that the Pod runs the new configuration. The two commands print the same value when it does:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pod <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.controller-revision-hash}'
   kubectl get sts <cluster-name>-mysql -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.status.updateRevision}'
   ```

1. Remove the file right away:

   ```bash
   kubectl exec <cluster-name>-mysql-<N> -n <namespace> -c mysql -- rm /var/lib/mysql/sleep-forever
   ```

   The container restarts, starts `mysqld` with the new configuration, and the Pod rejoins the cluster.

Warning

Remove the file as soon as the Pod runs the new configuration. With the `SmartUpdate` strategy, the Operator updates the primary Pod last. Before that, it switches the primary role to the first `Ready` secondary Pod. The Operator may choose the Pod with the `sleep-forever` file, and the switchover fails because `mysqld` doesn’t run there.
# Reference

# Custom Resource options reference

Percona Operator for MySQL uses [Custom Resources](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/api-extension/custom-resources/) to manage options for the various components of the cluster.

- `PerconaServerMySQL` Custom Resource with options for the cluster,
- `PerconaServerMySQLClusterSet` Custom Resource with options for InnoDB ClusterSet — see [ClusterSet Resource options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/clusterset-cr.md) and [cross-site replication](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/replication.md),
- `PerconaServerMySQLBackup` Custom Resource contains options for Percona XtraBackup used to backup Percona Server for MySQL
- `PerconaServerMySQLRestore` Custom Resource contains options for restoring Percona Server for MySQL from backups.

For status fields and conditions, see [Custom resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/cr-statuses.md).

## PerconaServerMySQL Custom Resource options

Percona Server for MySQL managed by the Operator is configured via the spec section of the [deploy/cr.yaml](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator/blob/v1.3.0/deploy/cr.yaml) file.

The metadata part of PerconaServerMySQL Custom Resource contains the following keys:

- `name` (`ps-cluster1` by default) sets the name of your Percona Server for MySQL cluster; it should include only [URL-compatible characters](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-2.3) , not exceed 22 characters, start with an alphabetic character, and end with an alphanumeric character;

- `finalizers` subsection:

  - `percona.com/delete-mysql-pods-in-order` if present, activates the [Finalizer](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/custom-resources/custom-resource-definitions/#finalizers) which controls the proper Pods deletion order in case of the cluster deletion event (on by default).
  - `percona.com/delete-mysql-pvc` if present, activates the [Finalizer](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/custom-resources/custom-resource-definitions/#finalizers) which deletes [Persistent Volume Claims](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/) for Percona Server for MySQL Pods after the cluster deletion event (off by default). It also triggers deletion of user Secrets.
  - `percona.com/delete-ssl` if present, activates the [Finalizer](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/custom-resources/custom-resource-definitions/#finalizers) which deletes [objects, created for SSL](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/TLS.md) (Secret, certificate, and issuer) after the cluster deletion event (off by default).

The top-level spec elements of the [deploy/cr.yaml](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator/blob/v1.3.0/deploy/cr.yaml) are the following ones:

## Toplevel `spec` elements

The spec part of the [deploy/cr.yaml](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator/blob/v1.3.0/deploy/cr.yaml) file contains the following:

### `crVersion`

Version of the Operator the Custom Resource belongs to.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| string     | `1.3.0` |

### `metadata.annotations`

The [Kubernetes annotations](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/annotations/) metadata that you can set at a global level for all resources created by the Operator.

| Value type | Example                     |
| ---------- | --------------------------- |
| label      | `example-annotation: value` |

### `metadata.labels`

The [Kubernetes labels](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/) metadata that you can set at a global level for all resources created by the Operator.

| Value type | Example                |
| ---------- | ---------------------- |
| label      | `example-label: value` |

### `pause`

Pause/resume: setting it to `true` gracefully stops the cluster, and setting it to `false` after shut down starts the cluster back.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `enableVolumeExpansion`

Enables or disables [storage resizing with volume expansion](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/scaling.md#storage-resizing-with-volume-expansion-capability).

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

This option is deprecated and will be removed in version 1.5.0. Use the [`storageScaling.enableVolumeScaling`](#storagescalingenablevolumescaling) option instead.

## Storage scaling section

The `storageScaling` section in the [deploy/cr.yaml](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator/blob/v1.3.0/deploy/cr.yaml) file controls volume expansion and automatic storage resizing for MySQL PVCs. See [Scale storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/scaling.md#scale-storage) for usage details.

### `storageScaling.enableVolumeScaling`

Enables or disables [storage scaling / volume expansion](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/scaling.md#storage-resizing-with-volume-expansion-capability) with Volume Expansion capability.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `storageScaling.enableExternalAutoscaling`

Enables or disables the use of external volume autoscaler. When disabled, the Operator uses its own expansion logic with Volume Expansion capability.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `storageScaling.autoscaling.enabled`

Enables automatic storage resizing based on user-defined thresholds. Read more about this feature in [Automatic storage resizing](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/scaling.md#automatic-storage-resizing).

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `storageScaling.autoscaling.triggerThresholdPercent`

The percentage of the storage usage that triggers automatic resizing. Valid values are from 50 to 95. Default value is 80.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| int        | `80`    |

### `storageScaling.autoscaling.growthStep`

The amount to increase the storage during automatic resizing. Default value is `2Gi`.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| string     | `2Gi`   |

### `storageScaling.autoscaling.maxSize`

The maximum size to which storage can be automatically resized. Autoscaling stops when storage reaches this limit. Must be at least `1Gi`.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| string     | `10Gi`  |

### `allowUnsafeConfigurations`

Prevents users from configuring a cluster with unsafe parameters such as starting a group replication cluster with less than 3 or more than 9 Percona Server for MySQL instances. **This option is deprecated and will be removed in future releases**. Use `unsafeFlags` subsection instead. Setting `allowUnsafeConfigurations` won’t have any effect with the Operator version 0.8.0 and newer, and upgrading existing clusters with `allowUnsafeConfigurations=true` will cause everything under the [unsafeFlags](#operator-unsafeflags-section) subsection set to `true`.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

## Unsafe flags section

The `unsafeFlags` section in the [deploy/cr.yaml](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator/blob/v1.3.0/deploy/cr.yaml) file contains various configuration options to prevent users from configuring a cluster with unsafe parameters. \*

Warning

Once unsafe configurations are enabled, you cannot revert these settings simply by setting the same keys back to `false`. Any such changes will be ignored, so enable these options with caution.

### `unsafeFlags.asyncFailoverWithPossibleDataLoss`

Allows users to disable backups in a cluster with asynchronous replication. Without this flag, the Operator rejects such a Custom Resource, because a [zero-data-loss failover](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/failover-async.md) reads the failed primary’s binary logs from the `xtrabackup` sidecar, and the sidecar runs only when backups are enabled. With backups disabled, a failover promotes a replica without recovering the transactions that the failed primary has not yet replicated. The Operator records the `FailoverUnprotected` [event](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/cr-statuses.md#events).

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `unsafeFlags.backupNonReadyCluster`

Allows the Operator to run a backup from a healthy MySQL Pod when the cluster is not yet ready.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `unsafeFlags.mysqlSize`

Allows a cluster size that is outside the safe defaults for the replication type:

- **Asynchronous (`async`):** a single MySQL instance (`mysql.size: 1`). Size 2 or greater is allowed without this flag starting with Operator 1.3.0, including even counts.
- **Group Replication (`group-replication`):** an even instance count, or more than 9 instances.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `unsafeFlags.proxy`

Allows users to configure a cluster with disabled proxy (both HAProxy and Router).

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `unsafeFlags.proxySize`

Allows users to set proxy (HAProxy or Router) size to a value less than 2 Pods.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `unsafeFlags.orchestrator`

Allows users to configure a cluster with disabled Orchestrator even if asynchronous replication is turned on.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

### `unsafeFlags.orchestratorSize`

Allows users to set [orchestrator.size](#orchestratorsize) option to a value less than the minimum safe size (3).

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `false` |

## Extended cert-manager configuration section

The `tls` section in the [deploy/cr.yaml](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator/blob/v1.3.0/deploy/cr.yaml) file contains options that control how the Operator requests TLS certificates from [cert-manager](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/tls-cert-manager.md).

### `tls.SANs`

Additional DNS names (subject alternative names) to add to the TLS certificate that cert-manager issues.

| Value type | Example               |
| ---------- | --------------------- |
| subdoc     | `mysql-1.example.com` |

### `tls.issuerConf.name`

The name of the cert-manager issuer that signs the cluster TLS certificate.

When set, the Operator creates a `Certificate` that references this issuer and does not create its own CA chain. Use this to integrate with an existing organizational PKI. See [Use an existing ClusterIssuer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/tls-cert-manager.md#use-an-existing-clusterissuer) and [Use an existing namespace-scoped Issuer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/tls-cert-manager.md#use-an-existing-namespace-scoped-issuer).

| Value type | Example                     |
| ---------- | --------------------------- |
| string     | `special-selfsigned-issuer` |

### `tls.issuerConf.kind`

The cert-manager issuer type referenced by the cluster `Certificate`.

Supported values:

- `Issuer` (default) — namespace-scoped issuer in the database namespace.
- `ClusterIssuer` — cluster-scoped issuer. Use this when your platform team manages a cluster-wide issuer. See [Use an existing ClusterIssuer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/tls-cert-manager.md#use-an-existing-clusterissuer).

| Value type | Example         |
| ---------- | --------------- |
| string     | `ClusterIssuer` |

### `tls.issuerConf.group`

The cert-manager API group for the issuer referenced in `issuerConf`. Use `cert-manager.io` for built-in cert-manager issuers.

| Value type | Example           |
| ---------- | ----------------- |
| string     | `cert-manager.io` |

## Upgrade options section

The `upgradeOptions` section in the [deploy/cr.yaml](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator/blob/v1.3.0/deploy/cr.yaml) file contains various configuration options to control Percona Server for MySQL version choice at the deployment time and during upgrades.

### `upgradeOptions.versionServiceEndpoint`

The Version Service URL used to check versions compatibility for upgrade.

| Value type | Example                     |
| ---------- | --------------------------- |
| string     | `https://check.percona.com` |

### `upgradeOptions.apply`

Specifies how images are picked up from the version service on initial start by the Operator. `Never` or `Disabled` will completely disable querying version service for images, otherwise it can be set to `Latest` or `Recommended` or to a specific version string of Percona Server for MySQL (e.g. `8.0.32-24`) that is wished to be version-locked (so that the user can control the version running) |

| Value type | Example    |
| ---------- | ---------- |
| string     | `Disabled` |

## Percona Server for MySQL section

The `mysql` section in the [deploy/cr.yaml](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator/blob/v1.3.0/deploy/cr.yaml) file contains general configuration options for the Percona Server for MySQL.

### `mysql.clusterType`

The cluster type: `async` for [Asynchronous replication](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/replication.html) , `group-replication` for [Group Replication](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/group-replication.html) .

Starting with Operator version 1.3.0, you can change this value on a running cluster. The Operator converts the topology in place. The switch causes downtime. See [Change replication type](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/change-replication-type.md) to learn more.

| Value type | Example             |
| ---------- | ------------------- |
| int        | `group-replication` |

### `mysql.bootstrap.mode`

Controls whether the Operator forms a Group Replication cluster automatically on first start. Use `manual` for replica sites in [cross-site replication](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/replication.md).

| Value type | Example  |
| ---------- | -------- |
| string     | `manual` |

Supported values:

| Value            | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `auto` (default) | Pod-0 runs the `dba.createCluster()` function when no peers exist. The same behavior is when the value for `bootstrap` is not set.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `manual`         | Pod-0 configures MySQL for Group Replication but does not create a cluster. Pod-0 stays in the `NotReady` state until the ClusterSet controller runs `createReplicaCluster()`. Pod-1 and above do not start until Pod-0 is `Ready`. The Percona Server for MySQL cluster reports the `Initializing` state and the Operator sets the `AwaitingExternalBootstrap` status condition. |

### `mysql.autoRecovery`

Enables the Operator to recover the cluster automatically after a full cluster crash. Applies to clusters with Group Replication. If you omit the option, the Operator treats it as `false`. See [Recover from a full cluster crash](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/crash-recovery.md) and [the `full-cluster-crash` file](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/datadir-special-files.md#full-cluster-crash).

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `true`  |

### `mysql.vaultSecretName`

Specifies the secret for the [HashiCorp Vault](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault) to carry on [Data at Rest Encryption](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/encryption.md).

| Value type | Example             |
| ---------- | ------------------- |
| string     | `ps-cluster1-vault` |

### `mysql.size`

The number of the Percona Server for MySQL instances. This setting is required.

The safe range depends on `mysql.clusterType`. For `async`, use 2 or more instances (even counts are allowed). Size `1` requires [`unsafeFlags.mysqlSize`](#unsafeflagsmysqlsize). For `group-replication`, use an odd count between 3 and 9 unless you set that flag.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| int        | `3`     |

### `mysql.image`

The Docker image of the Percona Server for MySQL used (actual image names for Percona Server for MySQL 8.0 and Percona Server for MySQL 5.7 can be found [in the list of certified images](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/images.md)).

| Value type | Example                              |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------ |
| string     | `percona/percona-server:8.0.46-37.1` |

### `mysql.imagePullPolicy`

The [policy used to update images](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/images/#updating-images) .

| Value type | Example  |
| ---------- | -------- |
| string     | `Always` |

### `mysql.runtimeClassName`

### `mysql.startupProbe.initialDelaySeconds`

The number of seconds to wait before performing the [startup probe](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/) .

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| int        | `15`    |

### `mysql.startupProbe.timeoutSeconds`

The number of seconds after which the [startup probe](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/) times out.

The startup probe runs MySQL bootstrap. On an asynchronous replica, bootstrap includes the clone, so this value limits how long that clone can run.

When `spec.crVersion` is `1.3.0` or higher, the default is 604800 seconds (7 days). A `crVersion` older than 1.3.0 keeps the previous default of 43200 seconds (12 hours). A value you set here replaces the default. See [Set the clone stall timeout](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/env-vars-custom.md#set-the-clone-stall-timeout).

| Value type | Example  |
| ---------- | -------- |
| int        | `604800` |

### `mysql.startupProbe.periodSeconds`

How often to perform the [startup probe](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/) . Measured in seconds.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| int        | `10`    |

### `mysql.startupProbe.successThreshold`

The number of successful probes required to mark the container successful.

### `mysql.env.name`

Name of an environment variable for MySQL Pods. The `BOOTSTRAP_READ_TIMEOUT` variable controls the timeout for bootstrapping the cluster. The `BOOTSTRAP_CLONE_STALL_TIMEOUT` sets how long an asynchronous clone can go without progress before bootstrap stops it for clusters with `crVersion` set to 1.3.0 or higher. See [Set the clone stall timeout](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/env-vars-custom.md#set-the-clone-stall-timeout).

Read more about defining environment variables in [Kubernetes documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/define-environment-variable-container/) .

### `mysql.autoConfig.enabled`

Enables [automatic configuration tuning](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/autoconfig.md). The Operator calculates a full MySQL configuration based on the Pod resources, database workload profile, and MySQL version. Requires `mysql.resources` (CPU and memory) and `mysql.autoConfig.version` to be set.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `true`  |

### `mysql.autoConfig.loadType`

The workload profile used to calculate the configuration. If not set, the Operator defaults to `someWrites`.

See [Choose a workload profile](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/autoconfig.md#choose-a-workload-profile) for what each value means.

| Value type | Allowed values                                                 | Example      |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| string     | `mostlyReads`, `someWrites`, `equalReadsWrites`, `heavyWrites` | `someWrites` |

### `mysql.autoConfig.version`

The MySQL version the configuration is calculated for, in the `<major>.<minor>.<patch>` format. This option controls the parameters set for the selected Percona Server for MySQL version. The [`mysql.image`](#mysqlimage) option controls the image version to be deployed. The Operator reads these two values separately. You must keep `mysql.autoConfig.version` and [`mysql.image`](#mysqlimage) values in sync yourself. Read more in the [Keep the MySQL version in sync](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/autoconfig.md#keep-the-mysql-version-in-sync).

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| string     | `8.4.8` |

## HAProxy subsection

The `proxy.haproxy` subsection in the [deploy/cr.yaml](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator/blob/v1.3.0/deploy/cr.yaml) file contains configuration options for the HAProxy service.

### `proxy.haproxy.enabled`

Enables or disables [load balancing with HAProxy](https://haproxy.org) [Services](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/) .

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| boolean    | `true`  |

### `proxy.haproxy.size`

The number of the HAProxy Pods [to provide load balancing](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/expose.md#use-haproxy). Safe configuration should have 2 or more. This setting is required.

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| int        | `3`     |

### `proxy.haproxy.image`

HAProxy Docker image to use.

| Value type | Example                                                    |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| string     | `percona/perconalab-xtradb-cluster-operator:1.3.0-haproxy` |

### `proxy.haproxy.imagePullPolicy`

The [policy used to update images](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/images/#updating-images) .

| Value type | Example  |
| ---------- | -------- |
| string     | `Always` |

### `proxy.haproxy.schedulerName`

The name of a [Kubernetes scheduler](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/kube-scheduler/) used to assign HAProxy Pods to Kubernetes nodes. The `default-scheduler` means `kube-scheduler` is used. You can define your custom schedulers here.

| Value type | Example             |
| ---------- | ------------------- |
| string     | `default-scheduler` |

### `proxy.haproxy.priorityClassName`

The name of the Kubernetes [PriorityClass](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption/#priorityclass) , which is a way to assign priority levels to pods, helping the scheduler decide which pods to schedule first and which ones to evict last when resources are tight.

| Value type | Example         |
| ---------- | --------------- |
| string     | `high-priority` |

### `proxy.haproxy.nodeSelector`

[Kubernetes nodeSelector](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/assign-pod-node/#nodeselector) . It enables you to define node labels thereby ensuring that Pods will be scheduled onto nodes that have each of the labels you specify.

| Value type | Example         |
| ---------- | --------------- |
| label      | `disktype: ssd` |

### `proxy.haproxy.serviceAccountName`

The [Kubernetes Service Account](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/) for the HAProxy Pods.

| Value type | Example                                      |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| string     | `percona-server-mysql-operator-orchestrator` |

### `proxy.haproxy.podDisruptionBudget.maxUnavailable`

The number of unavailable Pods your cluster can tolerate during voluntary disruption. It can be either an absolute value or a percentage.

To learn more, see [podDisruptionBudgets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions/) .

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| int        | 1       |

### `proxy.haproxy.podDisruptionBudget.minAvailable`

The number of Pods that must remain available during voluntary disruption. It can be either an absolute value or a percentage.

To learn more, see [podDisruptionBudgets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions/) .

| Value type | Example |
| ---------- | ------- |
| int        | 0       |

### `proxy.haproxy.runtimeClassName`

Specifies the name of the [RuntimeClass](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/runtime-class/) resource used to define and select the container runtime configuration.

| Value type | Example    |
| ---------- | ---------- |
| string     | `image-rc` |

### `proxy.haproxy.tolerations`

Specifies the [Kubernetes tolerations](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/taint-and-toleration/) applied to HAProxy Pods allowing them to be scheduled on nodes with matching taints. Tolerations enable the Pod to tolerate specific node conditions, such as resource constraints being temporary unreachable, without being evicted immediately.

| Value type | Example                                |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------- |
| subdoc     | `node.alpha.kubernetes.io/unreachable` |

### `proxy.haproxy.imagePullSecrets.name`
