# Percona Operator for MySQL 1.3.0 (2026-10-29)

[Installation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/System-Requirements.md#installation-guidelines)

Percona Operator for MySQL brings production-grade automation to MySQL deployments on Kubernetes. It handles provisioning, scaling, backups, failover, and upgrades using declarative Custom Resources, thus reducing manual effort and human error. With built-in support for Percona XtraBackup, proxies such as HAProxy or MySQL Router, and Percona Toolkit, it ensures resilient, secure, and performant MySQL clusters.

This release adds automatic MySQL configuration tuning, a replication type switch on a running cluster (tech preview), encrypted binlogs for point-in-time recovery, ability to manage application users via the Custom Resource, security builds for the Operator you already run, and support for Percona Server for MySQL 9.7. It also provides a number of improvements for async clusters and ClusterSet improvements.

## What’s new at a glance

**MySQL configuration**

- [Automatic MySQL configuration tuning](#automatic-mysql-configuration-tuning) - run production-ready MySQL clusters with MySQL settings calculated based on the Pod’s CPU and memory, database version and workload
- [Apply dynamic MySQL configuration without restarts](#apply-dynamic-mysql-configuration-without-restarts) - change dynamic variables while the cluster is running

**Replication**

- [Zero data loss failover for asynchronous clusters](#zero-data-loss-failover-for-asynchronous-clusters) - ensure all data is kept when promoting a replica
- [Switch replication type on a running cluster (tech preview)](#switch-replication-type-on-a-running-cluster-tech-preview) - move between Group Replication and asynchronous replication in place
- [Size asynchronous clusters the way you use them](#size-asynchronous-clusters-the-way-you-use-them) - use an even number of MySQL instances
- [Improved bootstrapping behavior for async replication clusters](#improved-bootstrapping-behavior-for-async-replication-clusters) - let a clone finish while it keeps making progress
- [Rejoin ClusterSet replicas automatically or by annotation](#rejoin-clusterset-replicas-automatically-or-by-annotation) - the Operator handles rejoin of failed replicas to the ClusterSet. You trigger rejoin only when the ClusterSet replication channel is down
- [Track replication lag for InnoDB ClusterSet](#track-replication-lag-for-innodb-clusterset) - read replication lag from the ClusterSet status

**Backups and recovery**

- [Encrypted binlogs for point-in-time recovery](#encrypted-binlogs-for-point-in-time-recovery) - encrypt binlogs before they are uploaded
- [Point-in-time recovery for encrypted clusters](#point-in-time-recovery-for-encrypted-clusters) - increase security of your point in time recovery
- [Backup options for start and suspend deadlines](#backup-options-for-start-and-suspend-deadlines) - limit how long a backup waits to start or resume

**Security**

- [Use your existing cert-manager ClusterIssuer for TLS](#use-your-existing-cert-manager-clusterissuer-for-tls) - sign MySQL certificates with your ClusterIssuer
- [Use your own CA to verify TLS with S3-compatible storage](#use-your-own-ca-to-verify-tls-with-s3-compatible-storage) - keep TLS verification on with your CA
- [Rotate TLS certificates without restarting MySQL Pods](#rotate-tls-certificates-without-restarting-mysql-pods) - reload a new leaf when the CA stays the same
- [Security builds for the Operator you already run](#security-builds-for-the-operator-you-already-run) - receive a High or Critical vulnerability fixes without a version upgrade

**Operations**

- [Manage application users from the Custom Resource](#manage-application-users-from-the-custom-resource) - declare users, grants, and passwords in the cluster spec
- [Configurable leader election for the Operator](#configurable-leader-election-for-the-operator) - tune lease timing, or turn election off
- [Persistent logging](#persistent-logging) - keep the MySQL error log after a Pod restarts

**Platforms and MySQL versions**

- [Official support for DigitalOcean Kubernetes Service (DOKS)](#official-support-for-digitalocean-kubernetes-service-doks) - run the Operator on DigitalOcean Kubernetes
- [Support for MySQL 9.7](#support-for-mysql-97) - run a cluster on Percona Server for MySQL 9.7

## Important upgrade notes

Check the following before you upgrade the Operator to 1.3.0. The upgrade steps are in the [upgrade guide](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/update-operator.md).

### Leader election is enabled by default

Starting with version 1.3.0, leader election for the Operator Deployment is on by default. When you upgrade the Operator to version 1.3.0, you can disable it via the `PSO_LEADER_ELECTION_ENABLED` environment variable.

See [Configurable leader election for the Operator](#configurable-leader-election-for-the-operator).

### Enable backups on asynchronous clusters

Version 1.3.0 requires backups so a failover on an [asynchronous replication](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/architecture.md#asynchronous-replication-tech-preview) cluster can recover transactions from the old primary. An asynchronous cluster with [`backup.enabled`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/operator.md#backupenabled) set to `false` fails validation, and reconciliation stops.

The status shows an error like this:

```text
Invalid configuration: When 'mysql.clusterType' is set to 'async', 'backup.enabled' must be true unless 'unsafeFlags.asyncFailoverWithPossibleDataLoss' is enabled. Without backups a failover cannot recover the transactions stranded on the old primary
```

A cluster that was valid on Operator 1.2.0 hits this check after the upgrade. Before you upgrade, do one of the following:

- [Enable and configure backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups.md#configuring-backups), and set `backup.enabled` to `true`.
- Set `unsafeFlags.asyncFailoverWithPossibleDataLoss` to `true` to continue without backups. A failover then cannot recover transactions that remain on the old primary.

Group Replication clusters are not part of this check.

### Take a new base backup when point-in-time recovery is enabled

If point-in-time recovery (PITR) is enabled, a recovery from a backup taken before the upgrade can fail with the following error:

```text
54edf529-d2cc-11f1-aebd-668621c1d52d:1-94 --stop-datetime=2026-10-28T13:50:49]
2026-10-28T13:52:40.183741217Z 0 [Info] [Recovery] streaming binlog binlogs1/binlog.000001
2026-10-28T13:52:40.692443772Z 0 [Info] [Recovery] pitr failed: apply binlogs: mysql failed: exit status 1, stderr: ERROR 1396 (HY000) at line 1907: Operation ALTER USER failed for 'configurator'@'%'
```

Do one of the following:

- Take a new base backup after the upgrade. Use that backup as the starting point for later point-in-time recovery. This is the recommended option.
- Force the restore. Set [`pitr.force`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/restore-cr.md#pitrforce) to `true` on the restore object. This passes `--force` to the MySQL client and ignores SQL errors during binlog replay, which can hide data loss. See [Ignore SQL errors during binlog replay](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-restore-pitr.md#ignore-sql-errors-during-binlog-replay).

## Release highlights

### Automatic MySQL configuration tuning

By default, the Operator tunes only two settings from the MySQL Pod’s memory limit: `innodb_buffer_pool_size` and `max_connections`. Every other setting uses the same server default, unless a database administrator (DBA) sets it by hand. Without that tuning, a cluster either keeps defaults that don’t align with the Pod’s allocated resources, or runs on manual settings that go stale when someone resizes the Pod.

Starting with version 1.3.0, the Operator calculates a MySQL configuration from the Pod’s CPU and memory, the workload you run, and the MySQL version. The calculation covers the InnoDB buffer pool and redo log, session buffers, connection limits, and replication settings for the cluster type you run. When you change the Pod’s resources or the workload, the Operator calculates those settings again.

The automatic configuration tuning is enabled for new clusters deployed with Operator 1.3.0 and `crVersion` 1.3.0 or higher. On a cluster you upgrade, turn it on in the Custom Resource.

With MySQL configuration calculated automatically, you:

- Have MySQL settings matched to the Pod’s CPU, memory, and workload
- Use the resources you already allocate to the MySQL container efficiently
- Have an updated configuration when you change `mysql.resources` or the workload

If you define MySQL settings in `spec.mysql.configuration`, a ConfigMap, or a Secret, the Operator applies those settings and skips automatic tuning.

Read [Automatic configuration tuning](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/autoconfig.md) for the workflow, setup, and gotchas.

### Apply dynamic MySQL configuration without restarts

Until now, every MySQL option change in the Custom Resource, ConfigMap, or a Secret triggered a rolling restart. That is correct for static variables, but many MySQL settings are dynamic and can take effect with the `SET GLOBAL` command. Restarts on every change dropped connections, flushed buffer pools, and made peak-hour tuning risky.

The Operator now applies dynamic variables at runtime. Update `mysql.configuration` in the Custom Resource and the Operator runs `SET GLOBAL` on every ready Pod without restarting it. If you set the value yourself with `SET GLOBAL` from the Pod, the Operator does not overwrite it. To keep that change after a Pod restart, add it to the Custom Resource, ConfigMap, or a Secret. If the declared value already matches, there is no restart.

Static variables, runtime-blocked changes, and removed options still trigger a rolling restart. You can tune a busy cluster and respond to an incident without a configuration restart.

Learn more in the [dynamic configuration documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/options.md#dynamic-configuration).

### Zero data loss failover for asynchronous clusters

Asynchronous replication copies transactions to replicas with a delay. If the primary fails, for example after an out-of-memory kill or a hardware fault, the transactions it committed but hasn’t yet sent to any replica exist only in its binary log. Until now, promoting a replica in that situation meant losing those transactions.

Starting with version 1.3.0, the Operator and Orchestrator recover those transactions before promoting a new primary. The replica chosen for promotion fetches the binary logs it is missing from the failed primary and applies them. Only then does it become the new primary. The logs are read through the `xtrabackup` sidecar, so the failed primary’s Pod must be reachable and its data volume intact, but `mysqld` on that Pod can be down.

You decide what happens when recovery can’t finish. You set a timeout (one hour by default) and a policy for when it expires. By default, the cluster stays read-only until you act. Alternatively, you can let the Operator promote a replica and accept the possible data loss. You can also force a promotion yourself with an annotation. The cluster’s status conditions and events show whether a failover is in progress or blocked.

With zero data loss failover, you gain:

- No lost transactions on primary failure — the new primary has everything the failed primary wrote to its binary log
- Predictable outcomes — the cluster waits and then follows the policy you chose instead of promoting a replica that is behind
- Visibility — status conditions and events report the state of every failover
- Declarative setup — you configure it in the cluster Custom Resource, like the rest of the cluster

This feature requires backups to be enabled for the cluster. Asynchronous replication is a tech preview, so we don’t recommend it for production environments yet.

To learn more, read our [documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/failover-async.md).

### Switch replication type on a running cluster (tech preview)

Now you can switch between Group Replication and asynchronous replication on a running cluster. Change `spec.mysql.clusterType`, and the Operator completes the switch. You do not pause the cluster and bring it back yourself.

The Operator converts the topology in place: it tears down the old replication setup, recreates the MySQL and proxy workloads, and bootstraps the new type on the same PersistentVolumeClaims. Users, Secrets, and the HAProxy Service stay in place, so applications keep the same connection endpoint if they already use HAProxy.

Switching the replication type on a running cluster is in tech preview stage. Try it in a staging cluster before you use it in production.

Use the switch when you need to:

- Move to Group Replication for stronger consistency, native failover, or [InnoDB ClusterSet](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/replication.md). Before you switch from asynchronous replication to Group Replication, confirm every replica is caught up and take a backup from the primary. The Operator can overwrite transactions that exist only outside `mysql-0`.
- Move to asynchronous replication for lower write latency, more than nine MySQL instances, or to avoid Group Replication limits on large transactions.

If a switch from Group Replication to asynchronous replication fails during bootstrap, you cannot switch back. Make sure to make a backup before the switch. This way you can restore the cluster from that backup.

The switch causes downtime while Pods restart. It applies to the entire cluster.

Learn more in the [Change replication type](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/change-replication-type.md) documentation.

### Rejoin ClusterSet replicas automatically or by annotation

With this release, the Operator automates ClusterSet replica rejoin. If the replica is paused, stopped, or crashed, the Operator reboots and rejoins it. If the replica is healthy but the ClusterSet replication channel is down after a long primary outage, choose a safe window and trigger rejoin by annotating the ClusterSet Custom Resource. The Operator then creates a rejoin Job, tracks its progress, and removes the annotation. On failure, it deletes the job and emits the `ClusterSetMemberRejoinFailed` warning. After you fix the cause, you can retry.

You decide when to rejoin, and the Operator runs the Job. For the steps, see [Rejoin a replica cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/replication-setup.md#rejoin-a-replica-cluster).

### Track replication lag for InnoDB ClusterSet

You can now see how far a ClusterSet replica is behind the primary in ClusterSet status with `kubectl`, instead of connecting to MySQL Shell. Use it to:

- Confirm a replica is catching up before you run switchover
- Keep read traffic off a site that is still behind
- Spot growing lag as it happens

Learn more in [Custom resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/cr-statuses.md#per-member-cluster-status).

### Size asynchronous clusters the way you use them

Asynchronous replication uses a primary and replicas. The nodes do not form a voting group. When the primary fails, Orchestrator promotes a replica, so an even number of instances is a valid high-availability setup.

You can now set `mysql.size` to 2, 4, 6, or any larger even count on an asynchronous cluster without `unsafeFlags.mysqlSize`. A single-instance cluster (`mysql.size: 1`) still requires the flag, because there is no replica to fail over to.

Use the replica count that fits your workload. Orchestrator still requires an odd size of 3 or greater. Set [`unsafeFlags.orchestratorSize`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/operator.md#unsafeflagsorchestratorsize) to run fewer than 3 Orchestrator Pods.

Asynchronous replication remains a tech preview feature.

Learn more in [Architecture](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/architecture.md#asynchronous-replication-tech-preview) and [Horizontal scaling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/scaling.md#horizontal-scaling).

### Improved bootstrapping behavior for async replication clusters

When a replica joins or rejoins an asynchronous cluster, MySQL copies the data with a native InnoDB clone (`CLONE INSTANCE`). With this release, joining works as follows:

- The `pt-heartbeat` sidecar does not start during the clone. It queries MySQL and starts `pt-heartbeat` only after the clone is no longer in progress and the `sys_operator` database is present. The sidecar waits until the clone finishes. A finished clone also restarts MySQL Pods. If `pt-heartbeat` exits in that short window, the script starts it again in the same container. A process that ran for a while and then exits is still treated as a failure, and the container restarts.
- The clone no longer has a fixed time limit. Bootstrap polls clone progress and stops the clone only when it makes no progress for `BOOTSTRAP_CLONE_STALL_TIMEOUT` (default 900 seconds). A clone that keeps moving runs until it finishes. A frozen clone, or one that cannot be observed for the whole stall window, is stopped. That fails the startup probe, kubelet restarts the container, and the clone is retried.

This behavior applies to clusters with `crVersion` set to 1.3.0. The Operator ignores `BOOTSTRAP_CLONE_TIMEOUT` for those clusters. The fixed timeout remains only for clusters with `crVersion` older than 1.3.0.

To turn off the stall check, set `BOOTSTRAP_CLONE_STALL_TIMEOUT` to `0`. See [Define environment variables for cluster components](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/env-vars-custom.md) for guidelines.

### Encrypted binlogs for point-in-time recovery

Encrypted backups and data-at-rest encryption protect the database and the base backup. They do not protect the binary logs that the Binlog Server stores in object storage for point-in-time recovery. Those files are written in plaintext, which leaves a gap if you use S3-compatible storage without server-side encryption, or if you need the full recovery path encrypted.

You can now encrypt binlogs before Percona Binlog Server uploads them. Create a Kubernetes Secret with your encryption keys, reference it in the cluster Custom Resource, and set the storage encryption options. The Operator validates the Secret, encrypts each new file on the way to the bucket, and decrypts it during restore. Files already in the bucket stay as they are and are applied as-is, so you can turn encryption on without emptying storage.

During key rotation, keep all previous keys in the Secret. Keep the Secret in the cluster if you turn binlog encryption off, so the Operator can still read existing encrypted binlogs. If a key is lost, those files cannot be recovered.

Point-in-time recovery remains a tech preview feature.

To learn more, read [Binlog encryption](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-pitr.md#binlog-encryption).

### Point-in-time recovery for encrypted clusters

You can now restore an encrypted cluster to a specific point in time. The Operator uses your existing Vault Secret during restore, so tablespaces and binlogs stay encrypted, and you can still roll the database forward to the GTID or time you need.

Point-in-time recovery remains a tech preview. Read more in the [point-in-time recovery documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-pitr.md).

### Backup options for start and suspend deadlines

This release adds options for how long a backup can wait.

`backup.startingDeadlineSeconds` sets how long a backup can wait to start. The backup waits when the cluster is not ready, or when another backup for this cluster is still running. If the Operator does not create the Job before this time expires, the backup state becomes `Error`.

`backup.suspendedDeadlineSeconds` sets how long a suspended backup can wait to resume. The Operator suspends a backup when the cluster is unhealthy, and resumes it when the cluster is ready again. A resumed backup starts from the beginning. If the backup does not resume before this time expires, the Operator marks it `Failed` and deletes the suspended Job.

The default for both options is `0`, which means the Operator does not enforce a deadline. Set them in the cluster Custom Resource for every backup, or on a `PerconaServerMySQLBackup` object for one backup. The value on the backup object takes precedence.

```yaml
spec:
  backup:
    startingDeadlineSeconds: 900
    suspendedDeadlineSeconds: 900
```

Read [Set a waiting time for a backup to start](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups.md#set-a-waiting-time-for-a-backup-to-start) and [Suspend backups on an unhealthy cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups.md#suspend-backups-on-an-unhealthy-cluster) to learn more.

### Use your existing cert-manager ClusterIssuer for TLS

If you already run cert-manager with a cluster-wide issuer, you can point Percona Operator for MySQL at that `ClusterIssuer` resource. Percona Server for MySQL certificates are then signed under the same public key infrastructure (PKI) you use for the rest of the platform.

To use a `ClusterIssuer`, configure the cluster as follows:

```yaml
spec:
  tls:
    issuerConf:
      name: my-org-issuer
      kind: ClusterIssuer
      group: cert-manager.io
```

The Operator resolves the issuer by kind, creates the leaf `Certificate`, and lets cert-manager sign and renew it. The Operator does not create a separate CA or overwrite your issuer.

MySQL TLS then follows the same issuer, renewal, and trust policy as your other workloads. You keep one source of truth for certificates instead of an Operator-managed CA in every database namespace.

Learn more in the [cert-manager TLS documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/tls-cert-manager.md#use-an-existing-clusterissuer).

### Use your own CA to verify TLS with S3-compatible storage

You can now verify TLS to S3-compatible storage with the certificate authority (CA) your organization already trusts. That matters when you use certificates from your corporate PKI, and security policy does not let you skip certificate checks.

Create a Secret with the CA and reference it in the storage configuration. Keep TLS verification enabled. The Operator uses that CA for backups and restores. You can also use the same CA for point-in-time recovery (tech preview) by referencing it in the Binlog Server storage configuration.

```yaml
spec:
  backup:
    enabled: true
    storages:
      minio:
        type: s3
        verifyTLS: true
        s3:
          bucket: S3-BACKUP-BUCKET-NAME-HERE
          region: us-west-2
          credentialsSecret: ps-cluster1-s3-credentials
          endpointUrl: https://minio-service:9000
          caBundle:
            name: minio-ca-bundle
            key: ca.crt
    pitr:
      enabled: true
      binlogServer:
        storage:
          s3:
            bucket: my-binlogs
            credentialsSecret: my-s3-secret
            region: us-east-1
            prefix: binlogs
            endpointUrl: https://minio-service:9000
            caBundle:
              name: minio-ca-bundle
              key: ca.crt
```

With this configuration you get:

- TLS verification that stays enabled for S3-compatible storage
- The CA your organization already trusts
- The same check for backups, restores, and point-in-time recovery

Read more in [Configure TLS verification with custom certificates for S3 storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-storage.md#configure-tls-verification-with-custom-certificates-for-s3-storage).

### Rotate TLS certificates without restarting MySQL Pods

When you update the server certificate (the leaf) in the TLS Secret, the Operator reloads the updated leaf into running `mysqld` processes when the certificate authority (CA) stays the same. MySQL Pods stay up. Existing connections keep the previous certificate until they reconnect. New connections use the new one.

HAProxy, MySQL Router, and Orchestrator still restart, because they read certificates once at startup. Changing the CA still restarts MySQL Pods. If you replace the CA, follow the CA rotation procedure in the [Update certificates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/tls-update.md) documentation.

This change gives you:

- MySQL availability during routine certificate renewal
- Fewer database Pod restarts on a cert-manager schedule
- The same workflow: keep `ca.crt` unchanged and replace only `tls.crt` and `tls.key`, or let cert-manager renew the leaf

### Security builds for the Operator you already run

The Operator has access to your cluster credentials and configuration. A vulnerability in the Operator image can expose that data even when your MySQL cluster is fully patched.

Security builds close that gap on a release you already run. Apply the fix without waiting for the next Operator version or retesting a full upgrade. A security build is a new Operator image that fixes a High or Critical vulnerability in your current Operator version.

Each release now comes with the following tags:

- `1.3.0` is the original release. Use it for a standard deployment.
- `1.3.0-1` is the same release image with a numbered tag. Use it when you need a fixed digest.
- `1.3.0-2`, `1.3.0-3`, and later numbers are security builds of that release. Each numbered tag stays on its own image. The first security build is `1.3.0-2`.
- `1.3.0-latest` is the newest image for this release. The tag moves, and it points at the most recent image.

Only the Operator image is updated. Database cluster components stay on the versions from the original release. Vulnerabilities in those images are outside a security build.

To apply a security build, patch the Operator Deployment and set the image to the security tag you chose. This restarts the Operator Pod. The cluster keeps running.

Read more in the [security builds documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/security-builds.md).

### Manage application users from the Custom Resource

Previously, you could only create application users by connecting to MySQL after the cluster was ready and running SQL, or adding extra steps to your CI/CD pipeline. You can now declare users in the cluster Custom Resource and let the Operator create them, grant privileges, and rotate passwords.

For each user, set the name. Optionally, set the hosts they can connect from, the databases they can access, and the MySQL grants. Supply a password in a Secret, or omit it and the Operator generates one and stores it in the `<cluster-name>-user-<username>` Secret. Change the Secret to rotate the password. The Operator applies it on the next reconcile.

You can create users when you provision the cluster and update them the same way you update any other configuration.

Learn more in [Manage users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/users.md#create-users-in-the-custom-resource).

### Configurable leader election for the Operator

You can now tune leader election for the Operator Deployment with environment variables. This helps when leader election fails, for example in a high-latency or resource-constrained cluster.

Leader election is enabled by default. When you upgrade, you can turn it off with `PSO_LEADER_ELECTION_ENABLED` environment variable if the Deployment has one replica.

- Set `PSO_LEADER_ELECTION_LEASE_DURATION`, `PSO_LEADER_ELECTION_RENEW_DEADLINE`, and `PSO_LEADER_ELECTION_RETRY_PERIOD` to adjust lease timing.
- Set `PSO_LEADER_ELECTION_ENABLED` to turn leader election on or off.
- Set `PSO_LEADER_ELECTION_LEASE_NAME` to use a custom Lease for the leader lock.

Learn more about these environment variables in the [documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/env-vars-operator.md).

### Persistent logging

Container logs disappear when a Pod restarts, so the MySQL error log from a crash is often gone by the time you look. Now the Operator keeps that error log on the MySQL data volume and rotates it so the file does not fill the volume.

Each MySQL Pod runs two sidecars. The `logs` container uses Fluent Bit to collect the error logs and the `logrotate` container rotates those files. During a backup, Fluent Bit also tails the Percona XtraBackup log. Those files live on an emptyDir volume. The Operator does not rotate them, and they do not survive a restart of the MySQL Pod.

Persistent logging is on by default for a cluster with `crVersion` 1.3.0 or later. It covers MySQL Pods only. HAProxy, MySQL Router, Orchestrator, and Percona Binlog Server still write only to standard output.

Read [Persistent logging](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/persistent-logging.md) and [Log rotation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/logrotate.md) to learn more.

### Official support for DigitalOcean Kubernetes Service (DOKS)

DigitalOcean Kubernetes Service (DOKS) is now a supported platform. Every Operator release is tested on DOKS, so you can run the Operator on DigitalOcean-managed Kubernetes clusters.

To install the Operator on DOKS, read the [installation guide](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/doks.md).

### Support for MySQL 9.7

This release adds support for Percona Server for MySQL 9.7. The Operator supports the major functionality of this version.

## CRD changes

These are the Custom Resource changes since Operator 1.2.0.

### PerconaServerMySQL

New fields:

- `spec.mysql.autoConfig` sets automatic MySQL configuration tuning with `enabled`, `loadType`, and `version`. When tuning is on, the Pod needs CPU and memory resources, and `version` is required.
- `spec.users` declares application users with `name`, `hosts`, `dbs`, `grants`, `passwordSecretRef`, and `withGrantOption`. See [Manage users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/users.md#create-users-in-the-custom-resource).
- `spec.logcollector` adds persistent logging and log rotation. `logRotate.schedule` defaults to `0 0 * * *`. `image` is required when the section is set.
- `spec.backup.startingDeadlineSeconds` and `spec.backup.suspendedDeadlineSeconds` set how long a backup can wait to start or to resume. The same fields exist on `PerconaServerMySQLBackup`. See [Set a waiting time for a backup to start](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups.md#set-a-waiting-time-for-a-backup-to-start).
- `spec.backup.storages.<name>.s3.caBundle` and `spec.backup.pitr.binlogServer.storage.s3.caBundle` name the Secret that holds your CA. `key` defaults to `ca.crt`. See [Configure TLS verification with custom certificates for S3 storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-storage.md#configure-tls-verification-with-custom-certificates-for-s3-storage).
- `spec.backup.pitr.binlogServer.storage.encryption` sets binlog encryption. `cipher` defaults to `AES-256-CTR`. `spec.backup.pitr.binlogServer.keyringSecret` is required when encryption is set. `key` defaults to `keyring.json`.
- `spec.orchestrator.failover` sets asynchronous failover behavior. `timeout` defaults to `1h`. `onTimeout` is `Abort` or `ForceWithPossibleDataLoss` and defaults to `Abort`. This section is valid only when `mysql.clusterType` is `async`.
- `spec.pmm.haproxyParams` passes HAProxy parameters to the PMM client.
- `spec.unsafeFlags.asyncFailoverWithPossibleDataLoss` lets an asynchronous cluster run without backups. See [Important upgrade notes](#enable-backups-on-asynchronous-clusters).
- `status.clusterType` reports the replication type the Operator last observed.

Validation changes:

- An asynchronous cluster can use `mysql.size` of 2 or greater, including an even count, without `unsafeFlags.mysqlSize`. Size 1 still requires that flag.
- Group Replication rejects an even `mysql.size` unless `unsafeFlags.mysqlSize` is `true`. The minimum stays 3, and a size above 9 still requires the flag.
- An asynchronous cluster requires `backup.enabled: true` unless `unsafeFlags.asyncFailoverWithPossibleDataLoss` is `true`.
- When you switch from asynchronous replication to Group Replication, `spec.orchestrator.enabled` must be `false`.
- `spec.tls.issuerConf` is an issuer reference with `name`, `kind`, and `group`, so you can point at a cert-manager `ClusterIssuer`. See [Use an existing ClusterIssuer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/tls-cert-manager.md#use-an-existing-clusterissuer).
- `spec.backup.storages` accepts at most 100 entries.
- `containerOptions.args.xtrabackup` accepts at most 100 arguments, and each argument can be at most 1024 characters. `--defaults-file` must be the first argument and use `--defaults-file=<path>`. `--defaults-extra-file` is rejected.

### PerconaServerMySQLBackup

- `spec.startingDeadlineSeconds` and `spec.suspendedDeadlineSeconds` override the cluster deadlines for one backup.
- `status.size` and `status.uncompressedSize` report the backup size after it succeeds. See [PerconaServerMySQLBackup status](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/cr-statuses.md#perconaservermysqlbackup-status).

### PerconaServerMySQLRestore

- `spec.backupSource` is its own object with `destination` and `storage`. It is no longer a copy of the backup status.
- `spec.pitr.keyringSecret` supplies the keyring Secret when you restore encrypted binlogs.
- `status.erroredGeneration` records the generation of a restore that ended in `Error`.

### PerconaServerMySQLClusterSet

- `status.clusters.<name>.replicationLagSeconds` reports how far a replica cluster is behind the primary. See [Per-member cluster status](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/cr-statuses.md#per-member-cluster-status).

## Changelog

### New Features

- [K8SPS-402](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-402) - Added deadlines for backups so you can limit how long a backup waits to start or to resume. Backups for one cluster still run one at a time, and the Operator marks a backup `Error` when the start deadline passes or `Failed` when a suspended backup does not resume.
- [K8SPS-408](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-408) - Added application user management in the Custom Resource so users, grants, and passwords are declared with the cluster. The Operator creates each user, applies the grants, and stores or rotates the password in a Secret.
- [K8SPS-500](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-500) - Added persistent logging, so the MySQL error log stays on the data volume after a Pod restarts. A `logs` sidecar streams that log to standard output, and `logrotate` rotates the files.
- [K8SPS-646](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-646) - Added an in-place switch between Group Replication and asynchronous replication on a running cluster (tech preview). Change `mysql.clusterType` and the Operator rebuilds the topology on the same volumes, with downtime while the Pods restart.
- [K8SPS-757](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-757) - Added support for a read-only root filesystem on the Percona Monitoring and Management (PMM) client sidecar. The Operator stores the PMM agent configuration on a writable volume, so the sidecar can start when the container root filesystem is read-only.
- [K8SPS-762](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-762) - Added security builds so you can patch a High or Critical vulnerability in the Operator image without upgrading to a new Operator version. Numbered tags such as `1.3.0-2` stay on a fixed image, and `1.3.0-latest` points at the newest image for your current release.
- [K8SPS-780](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-780) - Added support for Percona Server for MySQL 9.7 so you can run clusters on this long-term support release.
- [K8SPS-792](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-792) - Added a custom certificate authority (CA) for S3-compatible backup storage so TLS verification can stay on with your organization’s certificates.
- [K8SPS-823](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-823) - Added automatic MySQL configuration tuning with `mysql.autoConfig` so settings follow the Pod’s CPU, memory, workload, and MySQL version. Tuning is on for a new cluster. Any value you set in `mysql.configuration` still overrides the calculated setting.
- [K8SPS-849](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-849) - Added binlog encryption for point-in-time recovery so binary logs are encrypted before they are uploaded. The Operator validates the key Secret, encrypts each new file, and decrypts it during restore, while files already in the bucket stay unchanged.
- [K8SPS-943](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-943) - Added official support for DigitalOcean Kubernetes Service (DOKS) so you can run the Operator on DigitalOcean-managed clusters.

### Improvements

- [K8SPS-458](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-458) - Added HAProxy parameters for the PMM client so monitoring follows the proxy configured on the cluster. Set `spec.pmm.haproxyParams` to pass those parameters into the client.
- [K8SPS-471](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-471) - MySQL Pods now stay up when you rotate the server certificate and the certificate authority stays the same. The Operator reloads the new leaf into running `mysqld` processes, while HAProxy, MySQL Router, and Orchestrator still restart because they load certificates at startup.
- [K8SPS-504](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-504) - Orchestrator updates now follow SmartUpdate and restart other Pods before the leader. The topology service stays available during the rollout instead of dropping when the leader restarts first.
- [K8SPS-514](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-514) - The Operator now extends Orchestrator downtime on the backup source until the backup finishes. Orchestrator no longer ends that maintenance window mid-backup and fails over the Pod that is still being backed up.
- [K8SPS-528](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-528) - You can set `mysql.size` to an even number of two or greater on an asynchronous cluster without `unsafeFlags.mysqlSize`. A single-instance cluster still requires that flag because there is no replica to fail over to.
- [K8SPS-563](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-563) - Backup status now reports `status.size` and `status.uncompressedSize` after the backup succeeds. You can read the artifact size from `PerconaServerMySQLBackup` instead of checking object storage.
- [K8SPS-644](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-644) - Leader election is enabled by default, and its timing is configurable with Operator environment variables. Set `PSO_LEADER_ELECTION_ENABLED` to `"false"` on a single-replica Deployment, or adjust the lease duration, renew deadline, and retry period when election fails on a slow cluster.
- [K8SPS-652](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-652) - Disabled components no longer need an image and a size in the Custom Resource. A cluster that uses HAProxy no longer has to set MySQL Router fields, and the same applies to any other component you leave turned off.
- [K8SPS-678](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-678) - Incremental backups can use XtraBackup page tracking so only changed InnoDB pages are copied. Pass `--page-tracking` in the `xtrabackup` container options on the storage or the base backup, and the Operator installs the `mysqlbackup` component that tracking needs.
- [K8SPS-704](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-704) - `spec.backupSource` on a restore is now its own object with `destination` and `storage`. Restore manifests no longer reuse backup status fields that a restore does not apply.
- [K8SPS-726](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-726) - Point-in-time recovery now works with data-at-rest encryption. The Operator uses your existing Vault Secret during restore, so tablespaces and binary logs stay encrypted while you roll forward to a GTID or a time.
- [K8SPS-730](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-730) - The Operator now applies dynamic MySQL variables at runtime, so a change in `mysql.configuration` does not roll the Pods. A value you already set with `SET GLOBAL` on a Pod stays in place until you change the Custom Resource, and a matching value does not cause a restart.
- [K8SPS-746](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-746) - HAProxy no longer opens a separate external check for the replica, MySQL X, and admin backends. Those backends follow the primary check, which lowers the number of connections to MySQL.
- [K8SPS-753](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-753) - ClusterSet status now includes `replicationLagSeconds` for each replica cluster. You can read that lag with `kubectl` instead of connecting to MySQL Shell.
- [K8SPS-768](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-768) - The Operator automatically rejoins a ClusterSet replica that was paused, stopped, or crashed. When the replica is healthy but the replication channel is down, annotate the ClusterSet and the Operator runs the rejoin Job.
- [K8SPS-802](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-802) - The Operator now blocks deletion of a database cluster that still belongs to a ClusterSet. The Operator adds a finalizer so that delete does not leave the ClusterSet broken.
- [K8SPS-848](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-848) - The Group Replication liveness probe now treats a member in `RECOVERING` as alive. Kubernetes no longer kills the MySQL container while Group Replication is still catching up.
- [K8SPS-896](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-896) - A paused Group Replication cluster no longer writes a ClusterSet status skip message on every reconcile. That message is now a debug log, so the Operator log stays readable while the cluster is paused.
- [K8SPS-934](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-934) - Restores that end in the `Error` state are no longer run again when the Operator restarts. The Operator records `status.erroredGeneration` and skips that restore, so a restart does not pause the cluster or apply an unexpected backup.

### Bug Fixes

- [K8SPS-552](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-552) - Fixed asynchronous cluster creation on OpenShift when you set a custom Orchestrator service account. Reconciliation no longer fails with an owner-reference error on the Orchestrator Role, so the cluster can start.
- [K8SPS-649](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-649) - Fixed TLS issuer lookup so `tls.issuerConf.kind: ClusterIssuer` uses your cert-manager ClusterIssuer. The Operator previously looked only for an Issuer in the database namespace, so a cluster-wide issuer was ignored.
- [K8SPS-763](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-763) - Fixed XtraBackup argument order so `--defaults-file` is the first option on backup and restore. XtraBackup rejects that flag in any other position, and jobs that set it in `containerOptions.args.xtrabackup` now start.
- [K8SPS-782](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-782) - Fixed the HAProxy `mysql-x` backend so the primary is listed on the MySQL X Protocol port. The primary was registered on port 3306, so X Protocol clients through HAProxy did not reach it. (Thank you Wojciech Polnik for reporting this issue)
- [K8SPS-784](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-784) - Fixed HAProxy routing so only a current primary that can accept writes is placed in the writable backend. A replica that was made writable by hand is rejected, and a newly elected primary stays unavailable until it finishes applying events.
- [K8SPS-786](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-786) - Fixed Operator debug logs that printed Secret contents, including passwords, while updating the binlog server configuration. Secret data is omitted from those logs, and the configuration Secret is no longer rewritten on every reconcile.
- [K8SPS-791](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-791) - Fixed restore of a backup taken on a ClusterSet replica onto a new cluster. Bootstrap clears the leftover `clusterset_replication` channel, so creating the InnoDB Cluster no longer fails on that asynchronous channel.
- [K8SPS-830](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-830) - Fixed SmartUpdate so it continues when Pods are stuck Pending on an outdated spec. The Operator deletes those Pods and proceeds with the update instead of waiting until you delete them yourself.
- [K8SPS-840](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-840) - Fixed cluster status so a new reconcile error replaces the previous one when the cluster is already in an error state. `status.conditions` now shows the latest failure instead of an older message.
- [K8SPS-846](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-846) - Fixed `admin_address` selection so MySQL binds to the Pod’s routable address on IPv6 and dual-stack clusters. The entrypoint used the first address from `hostname -I`, which on Amazon EKS can be a non-routable link-local address. (Thank you Domantas Speciunas for reporting this issue and contributing the fix)
- [K8SPS-851](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-851) - The Operator no longer treats a minority Group Replication network split as a full cluster crash. Healthy Pods stay up when only some members lose connectivity. (Thank you Somanchi Poorna Sobhita for reporting this issue)
- [K8SPS-859](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-859) - Fixed an error loop that appeared when you resized PersistentVolumeClaims after scaling the MySQL cluster up and down. The Operator no longer retries that resize and logs a missing StatefulSet error on every reconcile.
- [K8SPS-863](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-863) - Fixed reconciliation that stalled after the MySQL StatefulSet was deleted while custom configuration was set. Applying dynamic variables no longer fails the reconcile when a Pod hostname is missing, so the Operator can recreate the StatefulSet.
- [K8SPS-866](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-866) - Fixed the `pt-heartbeat` sidecar crash with “Unknown database ‘sys_operator’” while an asynchronous replica is cloning. The sidecar now waits until the clone finishes and `sys_operator` exists before it starts.
- [K8SPS-871](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-871) - Fixed point-in-time recovery failures when the binlog list exceeded the 1 MiB ConfigMap limit. The Operator stores a smaller compressed manifest, so restore still works as the binlog history grows.

### Documentation updates

- Added the [Recover from a full cluster crash](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/crash-recovery.md) page. It explains how the Operator detects a full cluster crash on Group Replication, how recovery runs, and what to do when automatic recovery is off or does not succeed.
- Added troubleshooting pages for marker files in the MySQL data directory. [Special files in the data directory](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/datadir-special-files.md) describes each file. Use them to [pause a MySQL Pod](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/pause-mysql-pod.md), [pause a point-in-time recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/pause-pitr.md), or [unblock a stuck rolling update](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/pause-mysql-pod.md#unblock-a-stuck-rolling-update).

# Percona Operator for MySQL 1.2.0 (2026-07-03)

[Installation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/System-Requirements.md#installation-guidelines)

Percona Operator for MySQL brings production-grade automation to MySQL deployments on Kubernetes. It handles provisioning, scaling, backups, failover, and upgrades using declarative Custom Resources, thus reducing manual effort and human error. With built-in support for Percona XtraBackup, proxies such as HAProxy or MySQL Router, and Percona Toolkit, it ensures resilient, secure, and performant MySQL clusters.

## Release highlights

This release delivers key features such as cross-site replication, encrypted backups, and automated storage resizing, which harden the Operator for production use. Additionally, it improves security with Orchestrator API authentication and Vault encryption secret validation, and includes a bunch of improvements for day-to-day operations.

### Cross-site replication for Group Replication clusters

Until now, each Percona Server for MySQL cluster stood on its own. That worked well for high availability within a cluster where group replication keeps cluster nodes in sync. But to scale and span MySQL geographically for disaster recovery, migration or read distribution, you had to build and maintain custom tooling outside the Operator to interconnect sites and replicate data between them.

Cross-site replication closes that gap by linking Group Replication clusters into a [MySQL InnoDB ClusterSet](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/mysql-shell/8.4/en/innodb-clusterset.html) . You manage the topology declaratively from Kubernetes with a new `PerconaServerMySQLClusterSet` Custom Resource where you declare which clusters participate, which one is the primary, and how replicas receive data when they join the ClusterSet.

The Operator automates the ClusterSet provisioning and lifecycle management in a similar way it does for a standalone Percona Server for MySQL cluster. It bootstraps the ClusterSet, adds or removes replica clusters, refreshes status, and runs switchover when you change the primary. Because management runs over the MySQL protocol, replica clusters can run in the same Kubernetes cluster, a different cluster, or outside Kubernetes entirely.

With cross-site replication, you gain:

- Faster recovery — promote a live replica in a second region during an outage instead of restoring from backup alone.
- Regional read scaling — serve read traffic locally while writes stay on the primary.
- Unified operations — one Custom Resource and the same declarative model you already use for a single cluster.

Learn more about the workflow, setup and usage in the [cross-cluster replication documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/replication.md).

### Encrypted backups

You can now encrypt your backup data with Percona Operator for MySQL, so backup files stored in S3, GCS, or Azure are protected at rest. This helps you meet compliance requirements without adding external encryption tools or changing how you run scheduled and on-demand backups.

Encrypted backups are supported for both Group Replication and asynchronous replication cluster types.

The Operator uses Percona XtraBackup’s native encryption and automates the full workflow for you. You create a Kubernetes Secret with the encryption key and reference it in the cluster Custom Resource either on the global level or per storage. The storage-level setting takes precedence. The Operator uses that Secret to encrypt the backup stream during backup and to decrypt it automatically during in-place restore on the same cluster.

For a restore on a new cluster or in a different Kubernetes environment, provide the same encryption key in the restore resource, because the Operator has no access to Secrets from the source cluster. **The key used for the restore must match the key used to encrypt the backup**. If the key is lost, the backup cannot be recovered.

The default encryption algorithm is **AES256**. If your security policy requires a different cipher or you want to tune performance, you can override the algorithm and related settings through Percona XtraBackup options in `containerOptions.args.xtrabackup`.

To learn more about encrypted backups, read our [documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-encrypted.md).

### Automatic storage resizing

Starting with version 1.2.0, the Operator can automatically resize Persistent Volume Claims (PVCs) for Percona Server for MySQL Pods based on your configured thresholds. The Operator monitors storage usage and when it exceeds the defined threshold, triggers resizing until it reaches the maximum storage size.

This improvement gives you:

- Fewer outages from full disks because storage grows with demand
- Less guesswork in capacity planning and fewer last-minute fixes
- Lower operational effort for developers and platform engineers
- Cost control by expanding only when needed
- A more predictable environment so teams can focus on delivery

To enable automatic storage resizing, edit the Custom Resource manifest as follows:

```yaml
spec:
  storageScaling:
    enableVolumeScaling: true
    autoscaling:
      enabled: true
      triggerThresholdPercent: 80
      growthStep: 2Gi
      maxSize: "10Gi"
```

Learn more about the workflow and troubleshooting tips in our [documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/scaling.md#automatic-storage-resizing).

### Delegate PVC resizing to an external autoscaler

You can now configure the Operator to use an external storage autoscaler instead of its own resizing logic. This ability may be useful for organizations needing centralized, advanced, or cross-application scaling policies.

To use an external autoscaler, set the `spec.storageScaling.enableExternalAutoscaling` option to `true` in the Custom Resource manifest.

```yaml
spec:
  storageScaling:
    enableExternalAutoscaling: true
```

### Connection details exposed in the user Secret

Connecting applications to your cluster no longer means hunting down endpoints and credentials across Services and Secrets. With this release, the Operator creates and maintains a dedicated Secret for a `root` user that gives your application developers and administrators a single, reliable source of connection information. The Secret name follows the format `<cluster-name>-psuser-root` (`ps-cluster1-psuser-root` by default).

The Secret is owned by the Operator and updated on every reconciliation, so you always get current values without manual upkeep. The `host`, `port`, and `uri` fields point to the direct MySQL primary Service and are automatically updated when failover moves the primary to another Pod.

If you have enabled HAProxy or MySQL Router, the Secret also includes `proxy-host`, `proxy-port`, and `proxy-uri` values, so applications can connect through your proxy without extra configuration. These fields are generic — they do not reveal which proxy technology is in use.

When you expose the proxy with a `LoadBalancer` Service type and an external IP is assigned, the Secret adds `proxy-external-host`, `proxy-external-port`, and `proxy-external-uri` for connections from outside the cluster.

You can mount this Secret in your application Pods, reference it in your CI/CD pipeline, or use it with External Secrets. However you consume credentials today, you now have everything in one place.

### Configure binlog settings in the restore object for point-in-time recovery

You can now specify binlog storage directly in the `PerconaServerMySQLRestore` object when performing point-in-time recovery to a new cluster. Instead of configuring Binlog Server on the target cluster just to replay binary logs from the source environment, you define the binlog location alongside your existing `backupSource` settings. This simplifies the cross-cluster point-in-time recovery configuration as a single restore manifest carries everything needed for the operation.

When you trigger the restore, the Operator starts a temporary Binlog Server using those settings, uses it to locate and fetch the required binlogs from the object storage, and removes it when the restore completes.

This improvement makes the restore path straightforward. By separating binlog collection on the source cluster from binlog access during restore on the target, the Operator makes disaster recovery and migration scenarios much easier to plan and execute.

Point-in-time recovery remains a tech preview feature. We do not recommend using it in production environments yet, but we encourage you to try this workflow in staging or test clusters and share your feedback.

Read more about point-in-time recovery and restore to a new cluster in our [documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/backups-restore-pitr.md#restore-on-a-new-cluster).

### Disable NodePort allocation for LoadBalancer Services

By default, Kubernetes assigns a `NodePort` behind every `LoadBalancer` Service, even when the underlying load balancer does not require it.

With this release, you can now turn off `NodePort` allocation for the `LoadBalancer` Services created by the Operator. Update your cluster Custom Resource with the following configuration:

```yaml
spec:
  expose:
    type: LoadBalancer
    allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
```

This setting keeps the `LoadBalancer` Service behavior intact while preventing Kubernetes from reserving `NodePorts`. It’s useful when:

- Your load balancer implementation doesn’t rely on NodePorts
- You want to reduce the attack surface by avoiding unintended node level exposure
- You run many LoadBalancer services and want to avoid port exhaustion

### Independent resource configuration for HAProxy sidecar containers

HAProxy Pods include the `mysql-monit` sidecar, a lightweight DNS-polling container that monitors MySQL endpoints. Previously, it inherited resource requests and limits from the main HAProxy container. Since the sidecar needs far fewer resources than HAProxy itself, it was over-provisioned.

Now you can configure the resource requests and limits for each HAProxy sidecar container independently. Use the `spec.proxy.haproxy.sidecarResources` subsection in the Custom Resource and specify the required values for each sidecar:

```yaml
proxy:
  haproxy:
    sidecarResources:
      mysql-monit:
        requests:
          cpu: 50m
          memory: 64Mi
        limits:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 128Mi
```

This improvement helps you use cluster resources more efficiently and thereby lower your infrastructure costs.

### Vault encryption secret validation

The Operator now validates the Vault Secret when you enable data-at-rest encryption with HashiCorp Vault. If the Secret is missing or invalid, you see a clear error in the cluster status right away, so you can fix the configuration without digging through Pod logs.

With this validation, you can now deploy Vault and the database cluster together, such as using Helm integration charts. You can define the Secret reference up front and let the Operator wait until the Secret is present and valid before continuing cluster setup.

Read more about [configuring data-at-rest encryption with Vault](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/encryption-setup.md).

### Improve operational efficiency with the support for concurrent cluster reconciliation

Reconciliation is a Kubernetes mechanism to keep your cluster in sync with its desired state. Previously, the Operator ran only one reconciliation loop at a time. This sequential processing meant that other clusters managed by the same Operator had to wait for the current reconciliation to complete before receiving updates.

With this release, the Operator supports concurrent reconciling and can process several clusters simultaneously. You can define the maximum number of concurrent reconciles with the `MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES` environment variable for the Operator deployment.

This enhancement significantly improves scalability and responsiveness, especially in multi-cluster environments.

### Configurable DNS suffix for Operator connections

You can now specify a custom DNS suffix that the Operator uses when it generates service names. This is useful when the Operator runs in a vcluster or in a cluster with a custom DNS configuration. In those setups, the default `cluster.local` suffix can cause incorrect domain name resolution and, as a result, failed connections to external services such as PMM. By setting the `clusterServiceDNSSuffix` in the Custom Resource to your cluster’s DNS suffix, the Operator generates hostnames that match your DNS configuration. This ensures the service discoverability and correct communication between workloads.

### Secure Orchestrator API access with authentication

The Orchestrator HTTP API is the control plane for your MySQL clusters with asynchronous replication. It handles failovers, topology changes, and other critical operations.

Starting with this release, the Orchestrator API requires authentication. Clients must present valid user credentials to connect, and unauthenticated requests are rejected.

The Operator handles authentication automatically for its own API calls, reading credentials from the mounted secret, so day-to-day cluster management continues to work as before. For custom integrations or scripts that call the Orchestrator API directly, you will need to include the appropriate credentials.

This change hardens your deployment by ensuring only authorized callers can initiate failover or topology operations. As a result, you have a stronger protection against accidental or malicious disruption of your MySQL cluster.

### Fine-tune Orchestrator failover behavior

Until now, you could not adjust the Orchestrator behavior beyond the Operator defaults. This release makes the `spec.orchestrator.configuration` field effective, so you can tune failover settings per cluster directly in the Custom Resource.

Provide Orchestrator options as a JSON string. For example, with the `FailMasterPromotionOnLagMinutes` option, you can control how long Orchestrator waits before promoting a new primary when replication is lagging. Using the `RecoveryPeriodBlockSeconds` option, define how long to block recovery after a failover.

```yaml
spec:
  orchestrator:
    enabled: true
    configuration: '{"FailMasterPromotionOnLagMinutes": 30, "RecoveryPeriodBlockSeconds": 300}'
```

The Operator merges your settings into the Orchestrator configuration. When you change the `spec.orchestrator.configuration` field, Orchestrator Pods restart in a rolling fashion to apply the new settings.

Options that the Operator manages itself such as Raft topology, topology TLS, HTTP authentication, failover hooks, alias detection queries, and storage paths are reserved and ignored if you set them, so cluster automation continues to work reliably.

### Improved monitoring for clusters in multi-region or multi-namespace deployments in PMM

Now you can define a custom name for your clusters deployed in different data centers. This name helps Percona Management and Monitoring (PMM) Server to correctly recognize clusters as connected and monitor them as one deployment. Similarly, PMM Server identifies clusters deployed with the same names in different namespaces as separate ones and correctly displays performance metrics for you on dashboards.

To assign a custom name, define this configuration in the Custom Resource manifest for your cluster:

```yaml
spec:
  pmm:
    customClusterName: testClusterName
```

### Percona Server for MySQL clusters 8.4 have NUMA disabled by default

`innodb_numa_interleave` is a MySQL configuration variable that spreads memory allocation across multiple NUMA (Non Uniform Memory Access) nodes. MySQL 8.4 turns this setting on by default to improve performance on servers with NUMA architecture, particularly when using a large InnoDB buffer pool.

In Kubernetes, containers are not allowed to modify memory allocation policies due to common security restrictions. When MySQL tries to enable NUMA interleaving, Kubernetes blocks the request, which can lead to warnings or confusing log messages.

Because most cloud servers for Kubernetes use servers with only a single NUMA node, this MySQL setting provides no performance benefit in containerized environments. To keep MySQL behavior predictable and reduce unnecessary noise, the Operator now sets `innodb_numa_interleave` to `OFF` by default when it deploys Percona Server for MySQL 8.4. This reduces false alarms, and ensures MySQL runs smoothly in hardened Kubernetes environments.

You can still enable NUMA interleaving for your Percona Server for MySQL by passing custom MySQL options through the Operator. Be sure you understand the implications, as this requires a Kubernetes environment that allows NUMA policies.

### Documentation updates

Updated the README in the Helm chart to include the all available options.

## Deprecation, rename and removal

### Deprecated options

The `spec.enableVolumeExpansion` option is deprecated. It remains working for backward compatibility but it will be removed in version 1.5.0. Use the `spec.storageScaling.enableVolumeScaling` option instead.

## Known limitations

### Binlog Server image incompatibility notice

The new version of the Binlog Server image included in this release is not compatible with the previous version.

To upgrade the Binlog Server you must start a fresh binlog collection. Here’s how to do it:

1. Stop point-in-time recovery binlog collection
1. Create a new full backup
1. Change the binlog storage settings in your cluster configuration. It can be a new bucket or a new prefix for the existing bucket
1. Update the Binlog Server image
1. Re-enable point-in-time recovery

### Considerations for using OpenShift 4.22

Starting with OpenShift 4.22, the way images with not fully qualified names are pulled has changed for repositories that share the same repository name on DockerHub and Red Hat Marketplace. By default the tags are pulled from Red Hat Marketplace. Specifying not fully qualified image names may result in the `ImagePullBackOff` error.

- **OLM installation:** Images are provided with the fully qualified names and are pulled from the Red Hat Marketplace/DockerHub registry.
- **Manual install/update with default manifests:** Images must use the `docker.io` registry prefix to guarantee successful download from the DockerHub `percona-server-mysql-operator` repository.

For manual installation or update, follow the instructions below:

1. Clone the Operator repository:

   ```bash
   git clone -b v1.2.0 https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator
   cd percona-server-mysql-operator
   ```

1. Edit the `deploy/bundle.yaml` file.

   - Locate the Deployment custom resource for the Operator.
   - Update the `spec.image` field to

   ```text
   docker.io/percona/percona-server-mysql-operator:1.2.0
   ```

1. Apply the updated `deploy/bundle.yaml` file:

   ```bash
   oc apply --server-side -f deploy/bundle.yaml
   ```

1. Install Percona Server for MySQL:

   ```bash
   oc create -f deploy/cr.yaml
   ```

For the upgrade steps, follow the [Update documentation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/1.3.0/update-openshift.md#update-via-the-command-line-interface).

### New Features

- [K8SPS-127](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-127) - Added automatic storage scaling that monitors PVC usage and triggers resizing when usage crosses your configured threshold. This helps prevent outages from full disks and reduces manual capacity planning by expanding storage only when it is needed.
- [K8SPS-409](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-409) - Added encrypted backups to ensure backup data stored in S3, GCS, or Azure is protected at rest with a customer-controlled key.
- [K8SPS-496](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-496) - Added the ability to disable NodePort allocation for LoadBalancer Services created by the Operator when your load balancer does not need them.
- [K8SPS-508](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-508) - Added cross-site replication for Group Replication clusters with declarative topology management from Kubernetes via a new `PerconaServerMySQLClusterSet` Custom Resource.
- [K8SPS-512](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-512) - Added HAProxy version reporting in the cluster status so proxy version information is available from the start of the cluster lifecycle. This ensures telemetry and monitoring integrations receive accurate HAProxy version data instead of an empty value.
- [K8SPS-627](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-627) - Added the `pmm.customClusterName` option so you can assign a custom name to clusters monitored by Percona Monitoring and Management (PMM). PMM can now correctly group source and replica clusters across regions or namespaces as a single deployment on dashboards.
- [K8SPS-689](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-689) - Added a dedicated root user Secret that exposes connection details for your cluster in a single, operator-maintained resource.

### Improvements

- [K8SPS-19](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-19) - Enabled authentication for the Orchestrator HTTP API so only authorized clients can trigger failovers or topology changes. The Operator handles credentials automatically for its own calls, while custom scripts that access the API directly must provide valid credentials.
- [K8SPS-434](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-434) - Introduce the ability to configure the maximum number of concurrent reconciles via an environment variable so that the Operator can continue reconciling other clusters while an upgrade is in progress. This improves responsiveness in multi-cluster environments where a long-running upgrade previously stalled all other reconciliation work.
- [K8SPS-46](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-46) - Added the ability to pass custom Orchestrator configuration to the Operator without changing Operator defaults.
- [K8SPS-487](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-487) - Improved Vault encryption Secret handling by validating the Secret when data-at-rest encryption is enabled and reporting clear status errors when it is missing or invalid. This lets you deploy Vault and the database cluster together and see configuration problems immediately instead of digging through Pod logs.
- [K8SPS-497](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-497) - Improved graceful shutdown of the pt-heartbeat sidecar by handling SIGTERM in the entrypoint script. MySQL Pods now terminate faster during deletion or rolling updates instead of waiting for the full termination grace period while heartbeat keeps running.
- [K8SPS-503](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-503) - Improved Group Replication bootstrap logging to reflect clone-based recovery when `group_replication_clone_threshold` requires it. Bootstrap logs now match the actual recovery method, making troubleshooting less confusing for users.
- [K8SPS-525](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-525) - Added timestamps to failed backup Pod logs so you can tell whether a log entry belongs to the failed backup job or an earlier run. This makes it easier to correlate backup failures with the correct attempt when reviewing Pod or sidecar logs.
- [K8SPS-716](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-716) - Added ability to specify binlog storage through the `backupSource` field in the `PerconaServerMySQLRestore` object. You can configure point-in-time recovery to a new cluster from a single restore manifest without pre-configuring binlog storage on the target cluster.
- [K8SPS-742](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-742) - Added independent resource configuration for the `mysql-monit` sidecar container in HAProxy Pods via `spec.proxy.haproxy.sidecarResources`. You can set appropriate CPU and memory limits for the lightweight monitoring sidecar without over-provisioning it and save on infrastructure costs.

### Bug Fixes

- [K8SPS-296](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-296) - Improved the logging behavior for unhandled errors and stack traces that appeared when changing passwords in asynchronous replication clusters. Password rotation now completes cleanly without noisy reconciler errors in the Operator logs.
- [K8SPS-454](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-454) - Fixed an issue where MySQL cluster primary selection failed after a minor version upgrade, leaving all instances read-only with no primary. The Operator now handles post-upgrade topology recovery correctly so the cluster regains a writable primary. (Thank you Alexander Kuleshov for reporting this issue)
- [K8SPS-607](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-607) - Fixed reconciler errors that flooded Operator logs after deleting a `PerconaServerMySQLRestore` object. The restore controller now stops reconciling gracefully once the restore resource is removed.
- [K8SPS-638](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-638) - Fixed an issue where the Group Replication plugin and related configuration were loaded even when `spec.mysql.clusterType` was set to `async`. Asynchronous clusters no longer show Group Replication settings in Pod specs, logs, or configuration that were never requested.
- [K8SPS-680](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-680) - Fixed an issue where the `mysql-0` Pod could remain stuck in Terminating state until the termination grace period expired when deleting a cluster. Cluster deletion now completes promptly on affected platforms.
- [K8SPS-682](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-682) - Fixed an issue where the default enablement of NUMA interleaving in MySQL 8.4 caused container deployment errors under hardened security policies. The Operator now correctly restricts this option inside host VMs where MPOL_INTERLEAVE limits are active to guarantee pod initialization stability.
- [K8SPS-683](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-683) - Fixed the SmartUpdate behavior so that the Operator performs an explicit switchover before updating the primary Pod instead of deleting it directly. This applies to both Group Replication and asynchronous replication and reduces disruption during rolling upgrades.
- [K8SPS-686](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-686) - Fixed an issue where scheduled backups could start while a cluster was still initializing after a restore with `unsafeFlags.backupNonReadyCluster` enabled. Backups now wait until the database is ready again after restore completes.
- [K8SPS-699](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-699) - Fixed incremental backup restore when a failed backup exists in the chain by verifying the incremental chunk’s completeness when building the restore chain. Failed or incomplete incremental backups are now skipped to ensure the restore succeeds.
- [K8SPS-707](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-707) - Improved validation for the `spec.incrementalBaseBackupName` field to prevent specifying an incremental backup as the base one. The Operator now rejects invalid base backup references instead of creating an unsupported nested incremental chain.
- [K8SPS-709](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-709) - Fixed binlog server crashes when an S3-compatible bucket accumulated a very large number of objects over sustained operation. The Operator handles large binlog inventories more reliably so point-in-time recovery does not require manual bucket cleanup and Pod recreation.
- [K8SPS-739](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-739) - Fixed password propagation for MySQL Router clusters by using `Router.Size` instead of `HAProxy.Size` in the passwords-propagated check. Router-based deployments now receive credentials on all database Pods as intended. (Thank you user @jackiesre721 for contribution)
- [K8SPS-741](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-741) - Fixed a race when a partially pre-created user Secret caused the Operator to copy incomplete credentials to the internal Secret before auto-generating missing system user passwords. MySQL Pods now start reliably even when the user-supplied Secret contains only a subset of required keys.
- [K8SPS-744](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-744) - Fixed an issue where a custom `replica_parallel_workers` value in the cluster configuration was overridden to the default during bootstrap. The Operator now preserves your configured parallel applier thread count instead of resetting it to default value.
- [K8SPS-751](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-751) - Fixed Version Service request errors when `spec.upgradeOptions.apply` was not set in the Custom Resource. Clusters with telemetry enabled no longer generate repeated HTTP 500 errors against the version check endpoint on every reconcile loop.
- [K8SPS-755](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-755) - Fixed AutoRecovery bootstrap order so the Operator does not bootstrap `mysql-0` first when another Pod was the Group Replication primary before a full cluster crash. Recovery now respects the correct member order to avoid data loss after quorum loss.
- [K8SPS-760](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPS-760) - Fixed an Operator panic when `spec.backup` was omitted from the Custom Resource entirely. Clusters without a backup section now reconcile normally instead of crashing the controller. (Thank you Wilfried ROSET for contributing to this issue)
